   ┌──────────────────────────┐             ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 📦 POD   IP 10.244.1.5     │             │ 📦 POD   IP 10.244.1.8  (shared net)   │
   │  ┌────────────────────┐   │             │  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐    │
   │  │ 🐍 easypj-web        │   │             │  │ 🐍 easypj      │ │ 🌐 nginx       │    │
   │  │ Django gunicorn:8000│   │             │  │ Django :8000 │ │ static :80   │    │
   │  └────────────────────┘   │             │  └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘    │
   │                            │             │         │   localhost     │            │
   │                            │             │         └────────┬────────┘            │
   │                            │             │              ┌───▼────┐ shared 💾       │
   │                            │             │              │ volume │ (emptyDir)      │
   │                            │             │              └────────┘                │
   └──────────────────────────┘             └──────────────────────────────────────┘
   one container = the norm                   localhost:8000 = Django · localhost:80 = nginx
💡
Key pod facts
  • Every container in a pod shares the same IP
  • They talk to each other over localhost
  • Pods are ephemeral — replaced, never repaired
  • Never rely on a pod's name or IP — both change
🔧
Essential pod commands
  • kubectl get pods -o wide
  • kubectl describe pod <name>
  • kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>
  • kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh
easypj-pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-pod
  labels:
    app: easypj
    tier: web                # labels = how other objects find this pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: easypj
    image: easypj:v1
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "128Mi"        # scheduling floor (guaranteed)
        cpu: "250m"
      limits:
        memory: "256Mi"        # hard ceiling (OOMKilled if exceeded)
        cpu: "500m"
📖 Why "ephemeral" is the whole point

A bare Pod is a pet: delete it and it's gone for good — nothing recreates it, and its IP vanishes. That's exactly why you wrap pods in controllers (next) and why apps reach each other through Services (§4.4), never by pod IP. Treat pods as disposable cattle and Kubernetes' design suddenly makes sense.

Init Containers, Sidecars & the Pause Container

A pod can hold more than one container, and they don't all behave the same way. There are three roles worth knowing — and one hidden container you never write but always have:

KindWhen it runseasypj example
init containerBEFORE app containers, to completion, in order — the next won't start until it exits 0wait for easypj-db to accept connections, or run manage.py migrate
app containerThe long-running main process(es)gunicorn easypj.wsgi on :8000
sidecarALONGSIDE the app for its whole life (a special init container with restartPolicy: Always)an nginx static-file server, or a log shipper
🔒 pauseThe hidden "sandbox" — created first, holds the pod's network + IPC namespacesauto-created; app/sidecar containers join its namespaces
🩺 ephemeralInjected after the pod is already running, purely for debugging — never in pod.spec, never restarted, can't be removedkubectl debug -it easypj-web --image=busybox --target=easypj (full depth in Ch 6)
Pod startup order — init runs to completion, then the rest share the sandbox
   pod created
      │
      ▼  🔒 pause container starts → reserves the pod IP + network namespace
      ▼  ⏳ initContainer "wait-for-db"   runs → exits 0
      ▼  ⏳ initContainer "migrate"       runs → exits 0   (ordered, must succeed)
      ▼  ▶️ app: 🐍 easypj  +  sidecar: 🌐 nginx   start together, share the sandbox
   Running ✅
   ── if an init container fails → pod stuck in Init:0/2 → it never reaches Running
💡 Why init containers are the clean answer to "wait for X"

Instead of baking retry/wait logic into easypj's startup, an init container does the waiting (e.g. until easypj-db:5432 answers) and the app container starts only once the dependency is ready. And the pause container is why all containers in a pod share one IP: they all join its network namespace — so a crashing app container can restart without the pod losing its IP. You'll use init containers for real in Chapter 16 (Jobs/migrations).

The Three Named Multi-Container Patterns — Sidecar, Ambassador, Adapter

"Sidecar" above was really one instance of a family. Kubernetes documentation names three canonical multi-container patterns — same mechanism (shared network + volumes), three different jobs the helper container does for the app:

📎
Sidecar

Extends or enhances the main container — runs alongside it for the pod's whole life. easypj: an nginx container serving Django's collected static files from a shared volume.

📡
Ambassador

A local proxy the app talks to on localhost, which forwards out to the real (often complex/remote) service. easypj: a local proxy on localhost:5432 that forwards to a sharded/replicated PostgreSQL cluster — Django just sees "a database on localhost."

🔌
Adapter

Transforms the app's output into a standard format for the outside world. easypj: a container that reads Django's plain-text logs and re-emits them as structured JSON for a cluster-wide log collector.

Same shared-network mechanism, three different jobs
   📦 POD (one IP, one localhost)
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  🐍 easypj (app)                                                       │
   │     │ writes static files ──▶ 📎 sidecar (nginx) ──▶ serves them       │
   │     │ talks to localhost:5432 ──▶ 📡 ambassador ──▶ real Postgres cluster │
   │     │ writes plain-text logs ──▶ 🔌 adapter ──▶ JSON out to log collector│
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   💡 the app container never knows the helper is there — that's the whole point:
      it talks to "a file", "localhost:5432", or "stdout" and the helper does the rest.
💡 Why this taxonomy is worth knowing (beyond naming things)

All three patterns exist because the pod's shared network + volumes let you bolt on capability without touching app code — easypj's Django code never needs a Postgres-proxy library or a JSON logging formatter; the sidecar/ambassador/adapter container handles it. This is also the exact mechanism a service mesh sidecar (Istio/Linkerd, §1.5) uses to add mTLS and traffic policy to every pod with zero app changes.

4.2 ReplicaSets — Maintaining the Count

A ReplicaSet keeps a desired number of identical pods running, using a label selector to know which pods are "its." If one dies, it creates a replacement — that's self-healing. You rarely create a ReplicaSet directly; a Deployment manages it for you.

ReplicaSet self-healing — always 3 replicas
   ReplicaSet easypj-web-rs   (replicas: 3, selector: app=easypj,tier=web)

   HEALTHY                        POD 2 CRASHES                  SELF-HEALED
   ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐          ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐          ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐
   │📦 1│ │📦 2│ │📦 3│          │📦 1│ │💀 2│ │📦 3│          │📦 1│ │🆕 4│ │📦 3│
   └────┘ └────┘ └────┘          └────┘ └────┘ └────┘          └────┘ └────┘ └────┘
   3/3 Running ✅                 2/3 ⚠️                          3/3 Running ✅
                                     │ RS: "want 3, see 2"          ▲ new pod created
                                     └──────────────────────────────┘
📖 ReplicaSet vs Deployment

A ReplicaSet only ensures count. A Deployment adds rolling updates, rollback history, and version tracking on top — and creates/owns the ReplicaSet for you. In practice you always use Deployments; ReplicaSets are the layer doing the actual self-healing underneath.

Where the Hash in a Pod Name Comes From — pod-template-hash

You've seen pod names like easypj-web-7f8b4-abc1 — that middle segment isn't random. When a Deployment creates a ReplicaSet, it computes a hash of the pod template (image, env, labels — everything that would produce a genuinely different pod) and stamps it onto the ReplicaSet's name and onto every pod it owns as the label pod-template-hash.

why the hash exists: one label per template version, forever
   Deployment easypj-web  changes image v1→v2
        │ computes a NEW hash for the changed template
        ▼
   🎛️ ReplicaSet easypj-web-7f8b4   pod-template-hash: 7f8b4   (OLD template — v1, now 0 replicas)
   🎛️ ReplicaSet easypj-web-9c2e1   pod-template-hash: 9c2e1   (NEW template — v2, scaled up)

   💡 the Deployment's own selector doesn't include the hash — but each ReplicaSet's
      selector DOES, which is exactly how two ReplicaSets can share a Deployment
      without ever fighting over the same pods.

⚠️ Never hand-edit pod-template-hash — it's Kubernetes' own bookkeeping for "which template version is this pod running," and it's what makes rollouts/rollbacks able to tell ReplicaSets apart cleanly.

🚨 The bare-pod adoption trap

A ReplicaSet doesn't just create pods matching its selector — it adopts any existing, unowned pod whose labels happen to match too. So a "harmless" throwaway debug pod labeled app: easypj can get silently swallowed into a Deployment's ReplicaSet count (and later killed when the RS decides it's now "one too many"). The rule: never label a one-off pod with the same labels a real Deployment's selector uses — give debug pods a distinct label (e.g. app: debug-tmp) instead.

📖 The legacy predecessor — ReplicationController

Before ReplicaSets, Kubernetes had ReplicationController (RC) — same job, but its selector only supported simple equality (key=value), not the richer matchExpressions (in/notin/exists) a ReplicaSet supports. RC still technically exists but is effectively legacy — every current tool, including Deployments, is built on ReplicaSet. You'll see the name in older docs/blogs; treat it as history, not something to use.

4.3 Deployments — Managing the Application Lifecycle

The Deployment is the standard way to run a stateless app. You declare desired state (image, replicas, resources); the controller makes it real and adds rolling updates, rollbacks, and revision history — by managing a chain of ReplicaSets.

Deployment ownership chain (old ReplicaSets kept for rollback)
   🚀 Deployment: easypj-web
   ├── manages ─▶ 🎛️ ReplicaSet  easypj-web-7f8b4  (current, v3)
   │                ├── owns ─▶ 📦 easypj-web-7f8b4-abc1
   │                ├── owns ─▶ 📦 easypj-web-7f8b4-abc2
   │                └── owns ─▶ 📦 easypj-web-7f8b4-abc3
   ├── keeps ──▶ 🎛️ ReplicaSet  easypj-web-6d5a2  (old v2, scaled to 0)
   └── keeps ──▶ 🎛️ ReplicaSet  easypj-web-5c3f1  (old v1, scaled to 0)
   💡 old ReplicaSets at 0 replicas = your instant rollback history.
🪆 In plain English — the wrapping (nesting) model

Pod, ReplicaSet, and Deployment aren't competing things — each wraps the one below and adds a single capability. Think Russian dolls, smallest inside — see the picture below.

Russian dolls — each layer wraps the one inside it
   🚀 Deployment        "give me rolling updates + rollback + history"
     └─ 🎛️ ReplicaSet    "keep exactly N copies alive"   (self-healing)
          └─ 📦 Pod      "schedule these container(s) together, one IP"
               └─ 🐋 Container   "run my easypj process"

You create the outermost doll (the Deployment) and it builds the rest. That's why you almost never make a bare Pod or a lone ReplicaSet — you'd give up the capabilities the outer wrappers add. Need a one-off task instead of a long-running app? Swap the Deployment for a Job (Ch 16): same Pod inside, different outer doll.

easypj-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  labels:
    app: easypj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj                  # ← MUST match the template labels below
      tier: web
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1                   # at most 1 EXTRA pod while rolling
      maxUnavailable: 0             # zero-downtime: never dip below desired
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj                 # ← MUST match the selector above
        tier: web
        version: v3
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: easypj
        image: easypj:v3
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "128Mi"         # scheduling floor (guaranteed)
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "256Mi"         # hard ceiling (OOMKilled if exceeded)
            cpu: "500m"

Pod Lifecycle — the Phases & Statuses You'll See

Pod phases + the STATUS column you read in kubectl get pods
   ┌─────────┐    ┌─────────┐    ┌───────────┐
   │ Pending │──▶ │ Running │──▶ │ Succeeded │ (exit 0 — Jobs)
   └────┬────┘    └────┬────┘    └───────────┘
        │              └──▶ ┌────────┐
        └──────────────────▶│ Failed │ (exit ≠ 0)
                            └────────┘
   STATUS column (what kubectl actually shows):
   ContainerCreating  image pulling / volumes mounting
   Running            at least one container up
   Completed          all containers exited 0
   CrashLoopBackOff   container keeps crashing (growing backoff)
   ImagePullBackOff   can't pull the image
   Pending            not yet scheduled to a node
   Terminating        being gracefully deleted
   Init:N/M           init containers still running
⚠️ Reading those statuses for the exam
  • Pending → scheduler can't place it (no fit), ResourceQuota, or unbound PVC
  • ImagePullBackOff → wrong image/tag, private registry without imagePullSecrets
  • CrashLoopBackOff → kubectl logs <pod> --previous for the crash reason
  • Init:0/1 → an init container is stuck — kubectl logs <pod> -c <init>

Deployment Operations (CKA Speed)

terminal — the rollout toolkit
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3   # fast create
kubectl scale deployment easypj-web --replicas=5                      # scale
kubectl set image deployment/easypj-web easypj=easypj:v4              # rolling update
kubectl rollout status deployment/easypj-web                         # watch it
kubectl rollout history deployment/easypj-web                        # revisions
kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj-web                           # roll back 1
kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj-web --to-revision=2           # to a specific rev
💡 The strategy knobs

maxSurge: 1 allows one extra pod during the update; maxUnavailable: 0 means never drop below the desired count → zero downtime. Deep dive (incl. canary/blue-green) in Chapter 13.

4.4 Services — Stable Network Endpoints

Pods get random IPs that change on every restart — so you can never point a client at a pod IP. A Service gives a stable virtual IP + DNS name and load-balances across the pods its selector matches (its "endpoints").

TypeReachable fromUse casePort
ClusterIPInside the cluster onlyInternal (the default)any
NodePortOutside, via <nodeIP>:portDev / testing30000–32767
LoadBalancerOutside, via a cloud LBProduction (cloud)any
ExternalNameDNS alias (CNAME)Point at an external hostn/a
Service types — who can reach each
   🔒 ClusterIP (default)        🚪 NodePort                  ☁️ LoadBalancer
   ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐
   │ in-cluster only   │         │ <nodeIP>:30080    │        │ cloud LB          │
   │ VIP 10.96.0.10    │         │      │            │        │ 203.0.113.50      │
   │      │            │         │      ▼            │        │      │            │
   │      ▼            │         │ VIP 10.96.0.11    │        │      ▼            │
   │ 📦 easypj  📦 easypj│         │      │            │        │ VIP 10.96.0.12    │
   └──────────────────┘         │      ▼            │        │      │            │
                                │ 📦 easypj 📦 easypj│        │      ▼            │
                                └──────────────────┘        │ 📦 easypj 📦 easypj│
                                                             └──────────────────┘
   all three pick a READY pod by label selector (app=easypj) and load-balance to it
easypj-service.yaml — ClusterIP + NodePort
# internal Service (default) — stable VIP inside the cluster
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-svc
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: easypj           # matches the pod labels
    tier: web
  ports:
  - port: 80              # the Service port (what clients call)
    targetPort: 8000      # the container port (gunicorn listens here)
---
# external dev access — same pods, reachable from outside the cluster
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-nodeport
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: easypj
    tier: web
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8000
    nodePort: 30080       # reachable at <nodeIP>:30080 (range 30000–32767)
terminal — expose fast (CKA)
kubectl expose deployment easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000          # ClusterIP
kubectl expose deployment easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000 \
  --type=NodePort --name=easypj-nodeport
kubectl get endpoints easypj-svc      # the pod IPs this Service routes to (empty = bug!)

Service DNS — How Pods Find Each Other by Name

Every Service gets an automatic DNS name from CoreDNS, so easypj-web can reach easypj-db without ever knowing its IP:

Service DNS resolution & cross-namespace access
   from a pod in the easypj namespace, all of these reach the DB Service:
     easypj-db                              ← same namespace (short)
     easypj-db.easypj                       ← name.namespace
     easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local     ← the full FQDN
   pattern:  <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local

   cross-namespace:  easypj-web (ns: easypj)  ──curl postgres.data.svc.cluster.local──▶
                     🐘 postgres Service (ns: data)
💡 Debugging DNS & endpoints

Service unreachable by name? Check CoreDNS (kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns) and test from a pod: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- nslookup easypj-db. Unreachable by VIP? Check kubectl get endpoints easypj-svc — empty endpoints = the selector doesn't match any ready pod (the #1 Service bug; full depth in Part 5).

Two More Service Behaviours Worth Knowing

Beyond the four types, two knobs come up constantly — especially the moment you hit stateful apps like easypj's database.

🎯
Headless Service (clusterIP: None)

No VIP, no load-balancing. DNS returns the individual pod IPs directly. This is what StatefulSets use so clients can address a specific replica by a stable name like postgres-0.easypj-db… (Ch 16).

📌
sessionAffinity: ClientIP

Pins a client to the same backend pod for a timeout window instead of load-balancing every request — useful for sticky sessions. Default is None (spread freely).

Services Without a Selector — Manually Wiring Endpoints

Every example so far has Kubernetes compute the endpoints for you from a label selector. You can also create a Service with no selector at all and manage its EndpointSlice yourself — the escape hatch for pointing a stable in-cluster name at something Kubernetes doesn't manage, like an external database or a service living in another cluster.

easypj-external-db.yaml — a selector-less Service pointing outside the cluster
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-external-db      # pods reach it as easypj-external-db, same as any Service
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 5432                  # NO selector — nothing auto-populates endpoints
---
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  name: easypj-external-db-manual
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/service-name: easypj-external-db   # ← links it to the Service above
addressType: IPv4
ports:
- port: 5432
endpoints:
- addresses: ["203.0.113.42"]   # the real, off-cluster database IP

💡 easypj's Django code never needs to know the real database address changed — it always talks to easypj-external-db:5432. This is also how a plain ExternalName Service (a CNAME, no proxying at all) differs: selector-less-with-EndpointSlice still gets a real ClusterIP and load-balancing; ExternalName is pure DNS aliasing with neither.

Naming Every Port — the Rule Multi-Port Services Must Follow

Every Service example above exposed one port. The moment a Service exposes more than one, each port entry needs a unique name — the apiserver rejects an un-named multi-port Service outright:

a Service exposing both HTTP and metrics
spec:
  selector: { app: easypj }
  ports:
  - name: http           # REQUIRED once there's more than one port entry
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8000
  - name: metrics
    port: 9100
    targetPort: 9100

📖 The names also make targetPort referenceable by name from the pod side (containerPort: { name: http }) instead of by number — handy when the container port might change without the Service definition needing to.

📖 How kube-proxy actually routes (iptables vs IPVS)

A Service VIP isn't a real interface — it's a rule. kube-proxy programs the node so traffic to the VIP is DNAT'd to a ready pod IP:

  • iptables (default): a chain of rules with random probability per endpoint — simple, but rule lookup is O(n) at thousands of services.
  • IPVS: a kernel load-balancer with hash tables — O(1), better at large scale, more LB algorithms (round-robin, least-conn).
  • nftables: the newer successor to iptables mode.

Check the mode: kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/kube-proxy | grep -i proxier. This is why "Services are slow at scale" historically meant "switch to IPVS" — but IPVS is deprecated as of v1.35, so on modern clusters the scale answer is nftables instead (Ch 18/34).

The Service Types Aren't Alternatives — They're Layers

The biggest unlock for remembering the four types: each external type is built on top of the one below it. A LoadBalancer contains a working NodePort, which contains a working ClusterIP — so every Service always has its internal VIP, no matter how it's exposed:

Each type = the previous type + one more door
   🌍 type: LoadBalancer      = NodePort  +  a cloud load balancer in front
   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  ☁️ cloud LB 203.0.113.9:80 ──▶ <nodeIP>:31234 on every node      │
   │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
   │  │ 🚪 type: NodePort        = ClusterIP  +  a port on EVERY node│  │
   │  │   <anyNodeIP>:31234 ──▶ the ClusterIP                       │  │
   │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
   │  │  │ 🔌 type: ClusterIP     = the base: internal VIP + DNS  │  │  │
   │  │  │   10.96.142.10:80 ──▶ ready pod IPs :8000 (endpoints) │  │  │
   │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
   │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
   └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   (ExternalName is the odd one out: no VIP, no proxying — just a DNS CNAME alias)

   💡 consequence: a LoadBalancer Service ALSO answers on <nodeIP>:nodePort and on its
      ClusterIP — three valid doors to the same pods. On bare metal (no cloud), a
      LoadBalancer simply sits <pending> forever and behaves as its NodePort layer.
💡 Why this matters on the exam & in production

Exam clusters are kubeadm (no cloud): asked to "expose externally," reach for NodePort — a type: LoadBalancer will hang <pending> (that's expected, not broken). And when debugging, test the layers inside-out: ClusterIP from a pod → NodePort from a node → the LB last. The failing layer names the broken component (endpoints → kube-proxy → cloud controller).

4.5 Namespaces — Virtual Clusters

Namespaces are logical partitions of one cluster — used to isolate teams and environments. Each can carry its own ResourceQuota, RBAC, and NetworkPolicy, so easypj-dev and easypj-prod live side-by-side without colliding.

Namespace isolation — the easypj example
   ┌──────────────────────────────── ☸️ CLUSTER ────────────────────────────────┐
   │  ┌─────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────┐                     │
   │  │ 🟢 easypj-dev         │        │ 🔴 easypj-prod        │                    │
   │  │  1 replica · DEBUG=on │        │  3 replicas · DEBUG=off│                   │
   │  │  low limits           │        │  high limits           │                   │
   │  └─────────────────────┘        └─────────────────────┘                     │
   │  ┌─────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────┐                     │
   │  │ 🔧 kube-system        │        │ 📊 monitoring         │                    │
   │  │  CoreDNS · kube-proxy │        │  Prometheus · Grafana  │                   │
   │  └─────────────────────┘        └─────────────────────┘                     │
   │  each namespace can have its OWN: ResourceQuota · RBAC Roles · NetworkPolicy │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The Four Built-in Namespaces

📦
default

Where objects land with no namespace set. Avoid it in production.

🔧
kube-system

Control-plane add-ons: CoreDNS, kube-proxy, metrics-server. Don't deploy apps here.

🌍
kube-public

Readable by all (even unauthenticated). Holds the cluster-info ConfigMap.

💓
kube-node-lease

Node heartbeat Lease objects — used for fast node-health detection.

terminal — namespace commands
kubectl create namespace easypj-dev
kubectl get namespaces
kubectl get pods -n easypj-dev
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-dev   # make it the default
kubectl get pods -A                                            # across ALL namespaces
⚠️ The #1 exam trap: wrong namespace = zero marks

Every CKA task names a namespace at the top. Create the resource in the wrong one and you score nothing even if it's perfect. Always pass -n <ns> or switch context first. Also know what namespaces don't isolate: nodes and cluster-scoped objects (PersistentVolumes, Nodes, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles) live outside any namespace.

ResourceQuota — Capping a Namespace

easypj-quota.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: easypj-quota
  namespace: easypj-prod
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "20"
    services: "10"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "5"
💡 ResourceQuota vs LimitRange

ResourceQuota caps the namespace total (all pods combined). LimitRange sets per-pod/container defaults & maxes. Use both: Quota bounds the team, LimitRange stops any single pod from being greedy (full depth in Ch 15/41).

4.6 Labels, Selectors & Annotations

Labels are the glue of Kubernetes — key/value tags that select objects. They wire Services→Pods, Deployments→Pods, NetworkPolicies and RBAC. Annotations look similar but are non-identifying metadata that never select anything.

🔖
Labels — for selection

Used by selectors to match & group. Keep them meaningful.

  • app: easypj
  • tier: web | db
  • env: prod
  • version: v3
📝
Annotations — for metadata

For tools & humans. Never used for selection.

  • description: "easypj job board"
  • owner: "team-alpha"
  • kubernetes.io/change-cause: "v3"
  • prometheus.io/scrape: "true"
How labels connect objects (the Service selector)
   🔌 Service easypj-svc  (selector: app=easypj, tier=web)
        │ matches pods whose labels include BOTH
        ▼
   ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
   │ 📦 Pod        │  │ 📦 Pod        │  │ 📦 Pod        │
   │ app: easypj  │  │ app: easypj  │  │ app: easypj  │
   │ tier: web    │  │ tier: web    │  │ tier: db     │  ← tier mismatch
   │ ✅ MATCHED    │  │ ✅ MATCHED    │  │ ❌ NOT matched│
   └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘
   💡 change a label and you change what's selected — the source of most wiring bugs.
terminal — label commands
kubectl label pod easypj-pod tier=web          # add a label to a live object
kubectl get pods --show-labels                 # see all labels
kubectl get pods -l app=easypj                 # filter by selector
kubectl get pods -l 'app=easypj,tier=web'      # AND
kubectl get pods -l 'app in (easypj, other)'   # set-based
kubectl label pod easypj-pod tier-             # remove a label (trailing dash)
📖 The easypj label convention

Throughout this guide easypj uses app=easypj · tier=web|db · version=vN. Consistent labels are what make Services, Deployments, NetworkPolicies, and kubectl -l filters all "just work."

The Recommended Labels (a Real Convention)

Kubernetes defines a standard set of app.kubernetes.io/* labels so tools (dashboards, Helm, meshes) can understand any app the same way. Our short app=easypj is fine for learning; the well-known set is what you'll meet in production:

Recommended labelMeaningeasypj value
app.kubernetes.io/nameThe application's nameeasypj
app.kubernetes.io/componentThe role within the appweb / db
app.kubernetes.io/instanceThis specific installeasypj-prod
app.kubernetes.io/versionThe app versionv2
app.kubernetes.io/managed-byWhat deploys itHelm / kubectl

Two Kinds of Selector

Selectors come in two flavours — know both, because Services/ReplicaSets use the first and you'll use the second on the command line:

🟰
Equality-based

Simple key=value (AND of all). What matchLabels in a Service/Deployment uses.

kubectl get pods -l app=easypj,tier=web
🔢
Set-based

in, notin, exists. More expressive; used in matchExpressions and rich queries.

kubectl get pods -l 'tier in (web,db),version!=v1'
kubectl get pods -l 'app'      # has the label at all
💡 matchLabels vs matchExpressions

In a Deployment/Service spec, selector.matchLabels is the easy equality form; selector.matchExpressions unlocks set-based rules (e.g. "tier in (web,db)"). Both compile to the same selection — use matchLabels unless you genuinely need the extra power.

4.7 The Object Relationship Map

This is the one picture to memorize — how every object you've met wires together into a running easypj. If you can redraw this from memory, you can read (and debug) almost any manifest.

How easypj wires together — the relationship map
   🌍 Ingress / 🚪 Gateway
        │ routes host/path
        ▼
   🔌 Service ──selector(app=easypj)──▶ 📦 Pods
        ▲                                  ▲ owned by
   🚀 Deployment ──manages──▶ 🎛️ ReplicaSet ─┘ creates
        │ the pod template references:
        ├─ ⚙️ ConfigMap   (envFrom — non-secret config)
        ├─ 🔒 Secret      (envFrom — credentials)
        ├─ 💾 PVC ──▶ PV ──▶ 🧱 StorageClass   (durable storage)
        └─ 🛡️ ServiceAccount  ◀── RBAC (Role + Binding) controls access
   🗂️ Namespace contains ALL of the above   ·   🧯 NetworkPolicy firewalls pod traffic
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   💡 LABELS are the glue: a Service finds Pods ONLY by matching labels — not by name or IP.
💡 How to use this map for troubleshooting

Almost every "it's not working" follows an edge of this graph: Service has no endpoints → the selector↔label edge is broken; pod can't read config → the ConfigMap/Secret edge; forbidden → the ServiceAccount/RBAC edge; data lost on restart → the PVC edge. Find the broken edge, fix that object.

4.8 Pod Lifecycle & Health Probes

A pod isn't simply "up" or "down" — it moves through phases, its containers have their own states, and probes decide whether it's Ready for traffic. This is the vocabulary behind every "why is my pod stuck?" task.

① Pod phases — .status.phase

PhaseMeaning
Pendingaccepted, not running yet — being scheduled, or pulling images
Runningbound to a node; ≥1 container running / starting / restarting
Succeededall containers exited 0 and won't restart (Jobs / one-offs)
Failedall containers terminated; at least one exited non-zero
Unknownthe node's kubelet can't be reached (usually a comms problem)

② Container states — .status.containerStatuses[].state

StateMeaning · what to read
Waitingnot yet running — the reason says why (ContainerCreating, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff)
Runningstarted — has a startedAt timestamp
Terminatedfinished — records exitCode (137 = OOM/SIGKILL, 0 = clean), reason, finishedAt

③ restartPolicy — Always · OnFailure · Never

PolicyRestarts when…Used by
Always (default)the container exits for any reasonDeployments / long-running services
OnFailureonly on a non-zero exitbatch Jobs that may retry
Nevernever — pod goes Succeeded/Failedone-shot tasks

🔁 Restarts use exponential back-off (10s, 20s, 40s … capped at 5 min). A container that keeps crashing shows CrashLoopBackOff — that's the back-off waiting, not an error in itself; read kubectl logs for the real cause.

④ Pod conditions — the path to Ready (and to a Service endpoint)

A pod's .status.conditions flip True in order. Only a Ready pod is added to its Service's endpoints — this is the answer to "pod is Running but gets no traffic."

conditions → endpoint membership
   PodScheduled ─▶ PodReadyToStartContainers ─▶ Initialized ─▶ ContainersReady ─▶ Ready ──▶ endpoints
   (got a node)    (sandbox + network ready)     (init done)   (all probes pass)  (serving)
      ✗ no node             ✗ CNI/sandbox              ✗ initContainer          ✗ Ready=False
      (taints/resources)      failed to come up          still running/failed     ⇒ removed

📖 PodReadyToStartContainers is the newer condition sitting between scheduling and init — it flips True once the pod's sandbox (the pause container) is up and its network is configured, i.e. the CNI has done its job. A pod stuck before this condition points at CNI/sandbox trouble; stuck after it but before Initialized points at a hanging/failing init container instead.

⑤ Termination — the graceful shutdown sequence

what happens on a pod delete
   1. apiserver sets metadata.deletionTimestamp         (pod → Terminating)
   2. pod removed from Service endpoints                 (stops new traffic)
   3. kubelet sends SIGTERM to each container            (app should drain & exit)
   4. grace period: spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds   (default 30s)
   5. still alive? → SIGKILL (forced)                    then cleanup

💡 Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to match how long easypj needs to finish in-flight requests, and handle SIGTERM in the app for zero-downtime rollouts. kubectl delete pod --grace-period=0 --force skips the wait — only for genuinely stuck pods.

⑥ Health probes — startup, liveness, readiness

Probes let Kubernetes act on app health (deep config is in Part 4; the concepts belong here):

ProbeQuestionOn failure
startuphas the app finished booting?holds off liveness/readiness; kills it if it never starts (good for slow JVMs/DBs)
livenessis it still alive (not deadlocked)?restarts the container
readinesscan it serve traffic right now?removes the pod from Service endpoints (no restart)

Each probe uses one of four methods: httpGet (HTTP 2xx/3xx), tcpSocket (port opens), exec (command exits 0), or grpc (gRPC health check, stable since v1.27); tuned with initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, failureThreshold.

Probe Tuning — the Timing Math That Decides When Kubernetes Acts

The probe type chooses what happens on failure; the timing fields choose when. Every probe shares the same five knobs, and one small formula predicts exactly when Kubernetes will restart (liveness) or de-route (readiness) a pod:

a fully-tuned liveness probe for easypj — every knob annotated
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /jobs/
    port: 8000
  initialDelaySeconds: 10   # wait 10s after container start before the FIRST check
  periodSeconds: 10         # then check every 10s
  timeoutSeconds: 1         # each check must answer within 1s (slow = failed!)
  failureThreshold: 3       # 3 consecutive failures → act (restart, for liveness)
  successThreshold: 1       # 1 success resets the failure count (must be 1 for liveness)
When does Kubernetes actually act? — the failure-detection formula
  worst-case time to action  ≈  initialDelaySeconds  +  (periodSeconds × failureThreshold)

  with the values above:   10s + (10s × 3) = ~40s from container start
  app hangs mid-life:              (10s × 3) = ~30s from the hang to the restart

  timeline (app deadlocks at t=0):
  t=0 ── hang ── t=10 probe ❌(1) ── t=20 probe ❌(2) ── t=30 probe ❌(3) → 🔄 RESTART
Tuning mistakeWhat you observeFix
liveness too aggressive (short delay/period on a slow-booting app)a restart storm: pod killed before it ever finishes starting → CrashLoopBackOff on a healthy appadd a startupProbe (it silences liveness/readiness until boot completes) or raise initialDelaySeconds
timeoutSeconds: 1 against a sometimes-slow endpointrandom "failures" under load → spurious restarts / endpoint flappingraise the timeout, or probe a cheap dedicated /healthz path instead of a real page
liveness and readiness probing the same deep dependency (e.g. the DB)DB blips → every pod restarts and leaves the Service at once — a self-inflicted outageliveness = "is this process alive" (shallow); readiness = "can I serve" (may include deps)
💡 The one-line design rule

Liveness shallow, readiness honest, startup generous. Liveness should only fail when the process itself is wedged (restarting won't fix a down database — it just adds churn); readiness may check dependencies since de-routing is cheap and reversible; and a startup probe with a generous failureThreshold × periodSeconds budget protects slow boots better than a huge initialDelaySeconds ever will. Deep probe practice lands in Part 4.

4.9 Rollouts, Service Ports, Label Rules & Resource Scope

The exam-critical details that make the §4.3–4.6 objects actually behave: how a rollout paces itself, how Service ports map, the exact label grammar, and which resources live inside a namespace.

① Deployment rollout mechanics

A Deployment's strategy is RollingUpdate by default (the alternative, Recreate, kills all old pods first = downtime). The roll is paced by two knobs, plus a history limit for rollback:

FieldDefaultMeaning
maxSurge25%extra pods allowed above desired during the roll (higher = faster)
maxUnavailable25%pods allowed down during the roll (0 = zero-downtime, needs surge)
revisionHistoryLimit10old ReplicaSets kept at 0 replicas for instant rollback
minReadySeconds0a new pod must stay Ready this long before it counts as "available" — dampens flapping rollouts
progressDeadlineSeconds600 (10 min)if the roll hasn't made progress within this window, the Deployment reports Progressing=False — the automated "this rollout is stuck" signal
manage a rollout
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web easypj=easypj:v2   # trigger a rolling update
kubectl rollout status  deploy/easypj-web             # watch it progress
kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-web             # list revisions
kubectl rollout undo    deploy/easypj-web             # roll back to previous
kubectl rollout undo    deploy/easypj-web --to-revision=3
kubectl rollout pause|resume deploy/easypj-web        # batch edits into one roll

⚠️ The Deployment default is 25% / 25%. A DaemonSet differs: maxUnavailable defaults to 1, no surge by default. And a Deployment's .spec.selector is immutable after creation.

①b How a Deployment reports its own rollout health — status conditions

Beyond the pod-count numbers, a Deployment carries three .status.conditions that answer "is this rollout actually healthy?" — the same signal kubectl rollout status is reading under the hood:

ConditionTrue meansFalse/stuck means
Progressingnew pods are being created/becoming ready, on scheduleno progress within progressDeadlineSeconds — likely a bad image or failing probe blocking every new pod
Availableat least the minimum required replicas have been Ready for minReadySecondsnot enough healthy replicas right now
ReplicaFailure(absent/False normally)a ReplicaSet failed to create a pod (e.g. quota exceeded) — a distinct failure class from a bad rollout

See them directly with kubectl describe deploy easypj-web (the "Conditions" block) — this is the mechanism that turns a hung rollout from "wait and hope" into a specific, named condition you can alert on.

② Service ports — port vs targetPort vs nodePort

the three ports of a Service
   client ──▶ Service:PORT ──▶ TARGETPORT on the pod ──▶ app listening there
              (e.g. 80)         (e.g. 8000)               easypj on :8000

   NodePort type also opens:  <anyNodeIP>:NODEPORT ──▶ Service:port ──▶ targetPort
                              nodePort range 30000–32767  (auto-assigned if unset)

⚠️ targetPort must match the container's real port (easypj = 8000) or you get "connection refused" from a healthy-looking Service. port defaults to targetPort if omitted; a nodePort outside 30000–32767 is rejected.

③ Cross-namespace DNS — short name vs FQDN

Within one namespace, a pod reaches a Service by its short name (easypj-db). Across namespaces the short name fails — use the FQDN service.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Example: easypj-web in staging calling the DB in data → easypj-db.data.svc.cluster.local.

④ Label grammar & set-based selectors

A label key is [prefix/]name: an optional DNS-subdomain prefix, then a name ≤ 63 chars from a–z A–Z 0–9 - _ . starting/ending alphanumeric. Values follow the same ≤ 63-char rule (or empty). Selectors come in two forms:

FormExampleWhere
equality (AND)app=easypj,tier=webmatchLabels, kubectl -l
set — intier in (web,db)matchExpressions, -l
set — notintier notin (cache)matchExpressions
set — existstier (has it) · !tier (lacks it)matchExpressions / -l

⑤ Namespaced vs cluster-scoped resources

Some objects live inside a namespace; others are cluster-wide. Deleting a namespace deletes everything namespaced in it — cluster-scoped objects survive.

NamespacedCluster-scoped
Pod · Deployment · ReplicaSet · Service · ConfigMap · Secret · PVC · Role · RoleBinding · Ingress · NetworkPolicyNode · PersistentVolume · StorageClass · Namespace · ClusterRole · ClusterRoleBinding · CustomResourceDefinition

See which is which: kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true and kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false.

Under the Hood — ownerReferences, cascading deletion & how a Service finds pods

The relationship map isn't a metaphor — those edges are real fields in etcd. Understanding the actual links explains cascading deletes, "why did my pods come back," and empty endpoints.

① ownerReferences — the real parent-child links (and cascading deletion)

Each Pod a ReplicaSet creates carries an ownerReferences field pointing at that ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet points at the Deployment. That chain is what makes "delete the Deployment" also remove its ReplicaSets and Pods — garbage collection follows the owner links downward.

   🚀 Deployment easypj-web
        ▲ ownerReference
   🎛️ ReplicaSet easypj-web-7f8b4
        ▲ ownerReference
   📦 Pod easypj-web-7f8b4-abc1     (metadata.ownerReferences → the ReplicaSet)

   delete the Deployment → GC deletes the RS → GC deletes the Pods   (cascades down)
   delete a Pod only     → the RS sees "want 3, have 2" → makes a new one (why it "comes back")
GC / delete modeWhat happens
Background (default)Owner deleted immediately; children cleaned up in the background
ForegroundChildren deleted first, then the owner (owner shows "deleting" until done)
Orphan--cascade=orphan — delete only the owner, leave children running (adoptable later)
② The EndpointSlice controller — how a Service actually reaches pods

A Service doesn't hold pod IPs. The EndpointSlice controller watches pods matching the Service's selector and writes the list of ready pod IPs into EndpointSlice objects; kube-proxy programs those into the dataplane. That's the whole "selector → endpoints" mechanism — and why a label typo yields empty endpoints.

   🔌 Service easypj-svc (selector app=easypj,tier=web)
        │ EndpointSlice controller watches matching + READY pods
        ▼
   🗂️ EndpointSlice easypj-svc-x9k2 → [10.244.1.5:8000, 10.244.1.6:8000, 10.244.1.7:8000]
        │ kube-proxy programs iptables/IPVS
        ▼
   client → Service VIP → DNAT → one of those pod IPs
   ⚠️ selector ≠ pod labels, OR no pod passes readiness → EndpointSlice empty → 503/timeout
③ GVK / GVR & the RESTMapper — how kubectl resolves a "kind"

When you type kubectl get deploy, the client maps the short name → a GVK (Group/Version/Kind: apps/v1, Deployment) → a GVR (Group/Version/Resource: apps/v1/deployments) → the REST path /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/easypj/deployments. That's why every manifest needs apiVersion + kind, and how CRDs add brand-new kinds.

🔑 spec vs status. Every object splits into spec (your desired state — you write it) and status (the controller's report — you read it). Controllers reconcile spec→reality and write status back. kubectl get -o yaml shows both; you almost never edit status by hand.
④ Finalizers — why a "deleted" object gets stuck Terminating

Deletion isn't always instant. If an object has a finalizer (a string in metadata.finalizers), a delete doesn't remove it — it just sets deletionTimestamp and the object sits in Terminating until some controller finishes cleanup and removes its finalizer. Only when the list is empty does the API actually delete it.

   kubectl delete pvc easypj-data
        │
        ▼  API sets metadata.deletionTimestamp  (object now "Terminating")
        │  metadata.finalizers: [kubernetes.io/pvc-protection]   ← still present
        ▼  the responsible controller does cleanup (detach the volume…)
        ▼  controller REMOVES its finalizer from the list
        ▼  finalizers empty → API garbage-collects the object for real ✅
   ⚠️ controller gone/broken → finalizer never removed → object STUCK Terminating forever
🔑 The classic "stuck namespace." A Namespace stuck Terminating almost always means something inside it still has a finalizer (or an aggregated API is down). You diagnose with kubectl get ns <n> -o yaml (look at status + spec.finalizers) and fix the root cause — force-removing a finalizer is a last resort, since it skips the cleanup it was protecting.
🧹 Control the cascade — and the cross-namespace ownership rule

You can override the default deletion behaviour with --cascade, and ownership has one hard constraint:

   kubectl delete deploy easypj-web                       # --cascade=background (default): owner gone now, GC sweeps children
   kubectl delete deploy easypj-web --cascade=foreground  # children deleted FIRST; owner stays Terminating until they're gone
   kubectl delete deploy easypj-web --cascade=orphan      # delete the Deployment; LEAVE the ReplicaSet + Pods running
🔑 ownerReferences can't cross namespaces. A namespaced owner and its dependent must live in the same namespace (only a cluster-scoped object — e.g. a Node — may own across them). That rule is why deleting a namespace cleanly garbage-collects everything inside it.
🔗 EndpointSlice vs the legacy Endpoints object

The old Endpoints API packed every backend IP into one object — which became huge and churn-heavy for large Services. EndpointSlices shard them into pieces of ≤ 100 endpoints (so a 1,000-pod Service ≈ 10 small slices that update independently). EndpointSlices are the default; the legacy Endpoints API is now deprecated. Only Ready pods land in a slice — the exact mechanism behind "Running but receiving no traffic."

🔬 Deeper (exam + beyond): server-side apply tracks field ownership in managedFields so multiple actors (you, a controller, a GitOps tool) can co-own one object without clobbering each other; generateName lets the API mint unique names (how RS pods get their random suffix); and the spec/status split is itself a subresource (/status, /scale) with its own RBAC — which is how kubectl scale works without granting full edit.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Pod < ReplicaSet < Deployment — you create the Deployment; it owns the RS; the RS owns the Pods (via ownerReferences).
  • Pods are ephemeral — replaced not repaired; never rely on a pod name or IP.
  • Services give stable networking — a VIP + DNS name that load-balances to pods by label selector.
  • Namespaces isolate teams/envs — but NOT nodes or cluster-scoped objects (PV/Node/StorageClass).
  • Labels are the glue — Service↔Pod, Deployment↔Pod, NetworkPolicy, RBAC all wire by labels; annotations never select.
  • Only a Ready pod joins Service endpoints — conditions flip PodScheduled → Initialized → ContainersReady → Ready; a Running-but-not-Ready pod gets no traffic.
  • rollout undo is instant — it just scales a previous ReplicaSet (kept at 0 replicas) back up; revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) decides how many are kept.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Selector ≠ template labels. A Deployment's selector.matchLabels must match its pod-template labels, or it won't manage them; a Service's selector must match pod labels or endpoints are empty.
  • Deleting a Pod under a Deployment just respawns it — change the desired state (scale/delete the Deployment) instead.
  • Annotations aren't selectable. Put anything you need to match in labels, not annotations.
  • Wrong namespace = 0 marks. Always set -n / context first.
  • port vs targetPort. port is the Service's; targetPort is the container's (8000 for easypj). Mismatch = connection refused.
  • .spec.selector is IMMUTABLE on a Deployment/ReplicaSet — you can't edit it after creation; you must delete & recreate the object.
  • "Running but no traffic" usually means a failing readiness probe — the pod was removed from the Service endpoints without being restarted.
  • Namespace stuck in Terminating is almost always a finalizer holding a resource — find it, don't force it (Ch 1 UTH, Ch 32).
  • NodePort range is 30000–32767 — ask for anything outside it and the apiserver rejects the Service outright.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Generate, don't hand-write: kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 $do > d.yaml then edit.
  • Expose fast: kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000.
  • First Service check: kubectl get endpoints <svc> — empty = selector/readiness problem.
  • Change live objects: kubectl label / kubectl annotate; filter with -l.
  • Instant rollback: kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-web (add --to-revision=N after checking rollout history).

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 4)

the core-object toolkit
kubectl get all -n easypj                 # deploys, rs, pods, svc at a glance
kubectl get pods -l app=easypj -o wide    # filter by label
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3
kubectl expose deployment easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000
kubectl get endpoints easypj-svc          # does the Service find pods?
kubectl label pod easypj-pod tier=web     # label / annotate live objects
kubectl annotate deploy easypj-web note="rolled by ops"   # non-selecting metadata
kubectl explain deployment.spec --recursive   # in-exam field reference

# rollout lifecycle — the Deployment superpowers
kubectl rollout status  deploy/easypj-web  # watch a roll finish
kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-web  # list revisions
kubectl rollout undo    deploy/easypj-web  # instant rollback (--to-revision=N)
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web easypj=easypj:v2   # trigger a roll
kubectl scale deploy/easypj-web --replicas=5           # scale in place

# scope & deletion semantics
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true   # what lives in a namespace (false = cluster-wide)
kubectl delete deploy easypj-web --cascade=foreground  # children first | background (default) | orphan

🧠 Chapter 4 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (12)

Quick recall of the core objects — 12 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Pod vs Deployment — when would you create each?
Show Answer
Answer

Create a bare Pod only for a quick one-off/debug; for anything real, create a Deployment:

📦 bare Pod🚀 Deployment
Self-heals?no — gone for good if it diesyes (via its ReplicaSet)
Scale · roll out · roll back?noyes
Use fora quick one-off / debug podanything real
Explanation

A bare pod is a pet; a Deployment manages cattle. In practice you almost never create naked pods.

Q2
A Service has 0 endpoints. Give the two most common causes.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) The Service selector doesn't match any pod's labels. (2) Pods match but none is Ready (readiness probe failing). Confirm: kubectl get endpoints <svc> + compare selector to pod labels.

CauseHow to confirmFix
selector ≠ pod labelsget svc -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}' vs get pods --show-labelsalign selector or labels
no pod is Readyget pods → READY 0/1; describe → probe failuresfix the readiness probe / app
Explanation

Only ready, label-matching pods land in the EndpointSlice — both conditions must hold.

Q3
How do Namespaces isolate — and what do they NOT isolate?
Show Answer
Answer

They scope namespaced objects and can carry RBAC/Quota/NetworkPolicy — but cluster-scoped objects live outside any namespace:

✅ Namespaces DO scope❌ Namespaces do NOT scope
Pods · Services · Deployments · ConfigMaps · SecretsNodes
Roles · RoleBindings · ResourceQuota · NetworkPolicyPersistentVolumes · StorageClasses
(namespaced)ClusterRoles · ClusterRoleBindings · CRDs (cluster-scoped)
Explanation

Namespaces are a logical, not a hard security/physical, boundary — that's what NetworkPolicy + RBAC add.

Q4
Add the label tier=web to a running Deployment.
Show Answer
Answer
label a live object
kubectl label deployment easypj-web tier=web
kubectl label deployment easypj-web tier=web --overwrite   # change an existing value
# to label the PODS, edit the pod template — selectors match pod labels, not the Deployment's
Explanation

Labeling the Deployment object ≠ labeling its pods — the pod template's labels are what selectors match.

Q5
Label vs annotation — the difference and a use for each.
Show Answer
Answer
🔖 Label📝 Annotation
Purposeidentify & selectnon-identifying metadata
Selectable?yes — -l, matchLabelsnever
Exampleapp=easypjkubernetes.io/change-cause · prometheus.io/scrape
Explanation

If you need to match on it, it's a label. If it's just info, it's an annotation.

Q6
Name the ownership chain for a pod named easypj-web-7d4-x9k2.
Show Answer
Answer

The name literally encodes the chain; each layer links up via ownerReferences:

the ownership chain, read from the pod's own name
   🚀 Deployment   easypj-web
        │ owns (ownerReference)
        ▼
   🎛️ ReplicaSet   easypj-web-7d4            ← Deployment name + pod-template-hash
        │ owns
        ▼
   📦 Pod          easypj-web-7d4-x9k2       ← ReplicaSet name + random suffix
Explanation

The name literally encodes the chain — and that chain drives cascading deletion.

Q7
Why are Pods "ephemeral," and what's the implication for IPs?
Show Answer
Answer

A pod is never repaired — when it dies it's replaced by a new pod with a new name and a new IP. So you must never hard-code a pod IP; reach pods through a Service (stable VIP + DNS) instead.

pods churn; the Service address never does
  🔌 Service easypj-web   VIP 10.96.142.10  ·  DNS easypj-web.easypj.svc   ← STABLE, forever
        │ endpoints track whichever pods currently match + are Ready
        ▼
  t0:  📦 …-x9k2 (10.244.1.5)   💥 dies
  t1:  📦 …-m4p8 (10.244.2.9)   ← NEW name, NEW IP — clients never noticed
  ❌ hard-coded 10.244.1.5 → broken at t1      ✅ easypj-web (Service DNS) → always works
Explanation

This is the entire reason Services exist — stable networking over a moving set of pods.

Q8
List the 4 Service types and who can reach each.
Show Answer
Answer
TypeReachable byUse
ClusterIP (default)in-cluster onlyinternal service-to-service
NodePort<nodeIP>:30000–32767dev / bare-metal external access
LoadBalancera cloud load balancercloud production
ExternalNameDNS CNAME (no proxying)alias an external host
Explanation

ClusterIP for internal, NodePort for dev/bare-metal, LoadBalancer for cloud prod, ExternalName to alias something outside.

Q9
You delete a Pod managed by a Deployment. What happens and why?
Show Answer
Answer

The ReplicaSet immediately creates a replacement — its reconcile loop sees "want 3, have 2" and acts. To actually remove it, lower the desired state (kubectl scale) or delete the Deployment.

You doWhat changedController's reaction
kubectl delete pod …actual state only (3→2)gap detected → new pod created (back to 3)
kubectl scale --replicas=2desired state (3→2)no gap → the removal sticks ✅
kubectl delete deploy …desired state removed entirelycascade deletes RS + pods ✅
Explanation

You changed actual, not desired; the controller just closes the gap again.

Q10
From the relationship map: how does a ConfigMap reach a container?
Show Answer
Answer

The pod template references it three ways; the kubelet injects it when the container starts:

3 ways a ConfigMap reaches a container
# ① all keys → env vars
envFrom:
- configMapRef:
    name: easypj-config
# ② one key → one env var (optionally renamed)
env:
- name: DB_HOST
  valueFrom:
    configMapKeyRef:
      name: easypj-config
      key: db_host
# ③ keys → files in a mounted volume (can hot-reload)
volumes:
- name: cfg
  configMap:
    name: easypj-config
Explanation

Env values are fixed at start; file mounts can hot-reload. Full detail in Chapter 23.

Q11
What are the default RollingUpdate values, and what does each control?
Show Answer
Answer

maxSurge: 25% and maxUnavailable: 25% — the two knobs that pace a zero-downtime roll.

KnobControlsWith replicas: 4
maxSurgehow many extra pods may exist above desired during the rollup to 5 pods alive at once
maxUnavailablehow many of the desired pods may be down during the rollat least 3 always serving
Explanation

The analogy: changing tires while driving — maxSurge bolts a spare on first; maxUnavailable is how many wheels you'll briefly run without. The Recreate strategy skips the choreography entirely — and causes downtime.

Q12
A namespace is stuck in Terminating — likely cause, and how do you check?
Show Answer
Answer

A finalizer is blocking deletion — on the namespace itself or on a resource inside it whose controller can't finish cleanup.

find the blocker
kubectl get ns easypj-test -o yaml | grep -B2 -A6 finalizers   # what's holding it
kubectl get ns easypj-test -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'  # names the stuck resource type
kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name \
  | xargs -n1 kubectl get -n easypj-test 2>/dev/null            # anything left inside?
Explanation

Deletion sets deletionTimestamp, then waits until every finalizer clears. Fix the blocked resource/controller rather than force-stripping the finalizer (that can orphan real resources) — the full walkthrough is in Chapter 1's Scenario Q14 and Chapter 32.

⚙️ Chapter 4 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — produce the object or the fix with real commands.

Q1
Create a pod named web-pod in namespace production using the image nginx:1.25-alpine with the label app=web and a resource request of 100m CPU and 128Mi memory. Write the imperative command and the equivalent YAML.
Show Answer
Answer
imperative approach (generate yaml
# Imperative approach (generate YAML, then add resources)
kubectl run web-pod --image=nginx:1.25-alpine \
  --labels=app=web \
  -n production \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > web-pod.yaml

# Then edit to add resources, or use the full YAML:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-pod
  namespace: production
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web-pod
    image: nginx:1.25-alpine
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: "100m"
        memory: "128Mi"

# Apply it
kubectl apply -f web-pod.yaml
Explanation

This is a fundamental CKA task. The hybrid approach — imperative generation + declarative editing — is the fastest strategy. Key points: (1) kubectl run only creates pods (not deployments since v1.18+). (2) --dry-run=client -o yaml generates YAML without creating the resource. (3) Resource requests affect scheduling — the scheduler only places the pod on nodes with at least 100m CPU and 128Mi memory available. (4) Always create the namespace first if it doesn't exist: kubectl create namespace production.

Q2
What is the relationship between a Deployment, a ReplicaSet, and a Pod? If you create a Deployment with 3 replicas, how many of each object exist?
Show Answer
Answer

The hierarchy is: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods

bash
Deployment (nginx-deploy)
  └── ReplicaSet (nginx-deploy-7d4f6b9c8)     ← 1 ReplicaSet
        ├── Pod (nginx-deploy-7d4f6b9c8-abc12)  ← Pod 1
        ├── Pod (nginx-deploy-7d4f6b9c8-def34)  ← Pod 2
        └── Pod (nginx-deploy-7d4f6b9c8-ghi56)  ← Pod 3

Total: 1 Deployment + 1 ReplicaSet + 3 Pods = 5 objects

Ownership chain: Each object has an ownerReference pointing to its parent. Deleting the Deployment cascades down — deletes the ReplicaSet, which deletes the pods.

Explanation

Understanding this hierarchy is critical for CKA troubleshooting. Key points: (1) You should never create ReplicaSets directly — always use Deployments. (2) During rolling updates, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and scales it up while scaling the old one down. (3) Old ReplicaSets are kept (with 0 replicas) for rollback — controlled by spec.revisionHistoryLimit (default: 10). (4) If you see orphaned pods not managed by a Deployment, check for missing ownerReferences.

Q3
Explain the three Service types: ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer. For each type, describe who can access the service and provide an example command to create one.
Show Answer
Answer
Type Accessible From Port Range Use Case
ClusterIP Inside cluster only Any Internal services (DB, cache)
NodePort External via node IP 30000-32767 Dev/test external access
LoadBalancer External via cloud LB Any Production external access
clusterip (default)
# ClusterIP (default)
kubectl expose deployment nginx --port=80 --target-port=80

# NodePort
kubectl expose deployment nginx --type=NodePort --port=80 --target-port=80

# LoadBalancer
kubectl expose deployment nginx --type=LoadBalancer --port=80 --target-port=80
Explanation

Services provide stable networking for ephemeral pods. Each Service gets a permanent ClusterIP and DNS name. Key CKA concepts: (1) NodePort automatically creates a ClusterIP underneath — it's an extension. (2) LoadBalancer creates both ClusterIP and NodePort underneath. (3) The selector in the Service spec must match labels on the pods — if they don't match, the service has no endpoints. (4) kubectl expose is the fastest way to create a service on the CKA exam.

Q4
You create a Deployment with kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3. Now you need to update the image to easypj:v2. What command do you use, and what happens internally during the rolling update?
Show Answer
Answer
update the image
# Update the image
kubectl set image deployment/easypj-web easypj-web=easypj:v2

# Watch the rollout
kubectl rollout status deployment/easypj-web

# What happens internally:
# 1. Deployment controller creates a NEW ReplicaSet (easypj-web-v2-xxxxx)
# 2. Scales new RS up: 0 → 1
# 3. Scales old RS down: 3 → 2
# 4. Repeats until new RS has 3 and old RS has 0
# (controlled by maxSurge and maxUnavailable)
check rollout history
# Check rollout history
kubectl rollout history deployment/easypj-web

# Rollback if v2 is broken
kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj-web

# Rollback to a specific revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj-web --to-revision=1
Explanation

Rolling updates are a core CKA task. The Deployment's strategy.rollingUpdate settings control the pace: maxSurge (how many extra pods above desired count) and maxUnavailable (how many pods can be down during the update). Default is 25% for both. The old ReplicaSet is kept with 0 replicas so you can rollout undo. Pro tip: to record the change cause, add --record (deprecated but still works) or annotate the deployment with kubernetes.io/change-cause.

Q5
What are Labels and Selectors in Kubernetes? How do they connect Services to Pods? Give an example where a Service fails to route traffic because of a label mismatch.
Show Answer
Answer

Labels are key-value pairs attached to objects. Selectors are queries that match labels to connect objects together.

pod has label: app=web
# Pod has label: app=web
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-pod
  labels:
    app: web        # ← Label
    version: v1

# Service selects pods with app=web
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-svc
spec:
  selector:
    app: web        # ← Must EXACTLY match pod label
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

# ❌ BROKEN: Service selector doesn't match pod labels
spec:
  selector:
    app: frontend   # ← "frontend" ≠ "web" → NO endpoints!
diagnose: check if service has endpoints
# Diagnose: check if service has endpoints
kubectl get endpoints web-svc
# If ENDPOINTS shows <none>, selector doesn't match any pods
Explanation

Label/selector mismatches are one of the most common CKA troubleshooting scenarios. If traffic doesn't reach pods: (1) Check kubectl get endpoints <svc> — empty means no matching pods. (2) Compare kubectl get svc <svc> -o yaml | grep -A 5 selector with kubectl get pods --show-labels. (3) Labels must match exactly — app: web ≠ App: web (case sensitive). ReplicaSets and Deployments also use selectors to find their pods — same matching rules apply.

Q6
Create a Namespace called exam-prep, then create a Deployment named api-server in that namespace with 2 replicas of httpd:2.4. Finally, expose it as a NodePort service on port 80. Write all the imperative commands.
Show Answer
Answer
create namespace
# Step 1: Create namespace
kubectl create namespace exam-prep

# Step 2: Create deployment
kubectl create deployment api-server \
  --image=httpd:2.4 \
  --replicas=2 \
  -n exam-prep

# Step 3: Expose as NodePort
kubectl expose deployment api-server \
  --type=NodePort \
  --port=80 \
  --target-port=80 \
  -n exam-prep

# Verify everything
kubectl get all -n exam-prep

# Access the service
kubectl get svc api-server -n exam-prep
# Note the NodePort (e.g., 31234)
# Access via: http://<node-ip>:31234
Explanation

This 3-command sequence is a bread-and-butter CKA task. Timing tip: this should take under 60 seconds. Key points: (1) Always specify -n <namespace> or use kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=exam-prep to avoid mistakes. (2) --port is the service port, --target-port is the container port. (3) Kubernetes auto-assigns a NodePort from 30000-32767 unless you specify --node-port=XXXXX. (4) kubectl get all shows deployments, replicasets, pods, and services in one view.

Q7
What is the difference between kubectl create and kubectl apply? When would you use each one on the CKA exam?
Show Answer
Answer
Feature kubectl create kubectl apply
Type Imperative Declarative
If exists Error: "already exists" Updates (merges changes)
Idempotent No Yes
Best for First-time creation, speed Updates, CI/CD, repeatability
cka strategy: use create for speed, apply for edits
# CKA strategy: use create for speed, apply for edits
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > web.yaml
vim web.yaml  # add resources, probes, volumes
kubectl apply -f web.yaml

# Later, edit and re-apply
vim web.yaml  # change replicas, image
kubectl apply -f web.yaml  # applies only the diff
Explanation

On the CKA, use create with --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate quick scaffolds, then apply to submit them. If a question says "create," either works. If a question says "update" or "modify," you need apply or kubectl edit or kubectl patch. Pro tip: kubectl apply stores the last-applied configuration as an annotation, enabling three-way merge diffs on subsequent applies.

Q8
A pod is in Pending state. When you describe it, events show: "0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu". What does this mean and what are your options to fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

The scheduler cannot find any node with enough free CPU to satisfy the pod's resources.requests.cpu. Options to fix:

  1. Reduce the pod's CPU request:
    or edit the deployment
    kubectl edit pod <name>  # or edit the deployment
# Change resources.requests.cpu to a lower value
  2. Free up resources by deleting/scaling down other workloads:
    bash
    kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu | head -10
kubectl scale deployment heavy-app --replicas=1
  3. Add more nodes to the cluster to provide additional capacity
  4. Check ResourceQuotas — a namespace quota may be artificially limiting available resources:
    bash
    kubectl get resourcequota -n <namespace>
Explanation

The "Insufficient" message is from the scheduler's filtering phase. It checked all 3 nodes and none had enough allocatable CPU. On the CKA, kubectl describe pod events section is your best friend for diagnosing Pending pods. Other common Pending causes: node taints without matching tolerations, node selector/affinity not matching, PVC unbound (waiting for PV). Always read the specific message — it tells you exactly which filter failed and on how many nodes.

Q9
What are Annotations in Kubernetes? How do they differ from Labels, and when would you use annotations instead of labels?
Show Answer
Answer
Feature Labels Annotations
Purpose Identify and select objects Attach non-identifying metadata
Used in selectors Yes (selector: app=web) No
Size limit 63 chars value 256KB total
Example app: web, tier: frontend description: "Main web app"
add annotation
# Add annotation
kubectl annotate deployment web kubernetes.io/change-cause="Updated to v2"

# Add label
kubectl label pod web-pod tier=frontend

# Filter by label (annotations can't be used in selectors)
kubectl get pods -l tier=frontend
Explanation

Labels are for identification and grouping. Annotations are for metadata storage. Common annotations you'll see on the CKA: (1) kubernetes.io/change-cause — records why a rollout happened, (2) kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration — stored by kubectl apply, (3) Ingress controller annotations (e.g., nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target). The CKA may ask you to annotate objects or add labels for selection — know the syntax for both.

Q10
You need to scale a Deployment from 3 replicas to 5, then verify the rollout completed. What are three different ways to accomplish this on the CKA exam?
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl scale (fastest)
# Method 1: kubectl scale (fastest)
kubectl scale deployment easypj-web --replicas=5

# Method 2: kubectl edit (in-place edit)
kubectl edit deployment easypj-web
# Change spec.replicas from 3 to 5, save and exit

# Method 3: kubectl patch (JSON patch)
kubectl patch deployment easypj-web -p '{"spec":{"replicas":5}}'

# Verify (all methods)
kubectl rollout status deployment easypj-web
kubectl get deployment easypj-web
# Ready: 5/5
Explanation

kubectl scale is the fastest method for the CKA exam. However, kubectl edit is useful when you need to change multiple fields at once. kubectl patch is scriptable and good for automation. Key insight: scaling does NOT trigger a rollout — it only changes the replica count on the current ReplicaSet. Only image changes, env changes, or other spec updates trigger new rollouts. Verify scaling with kubectl get deployment — check that READY shows 5/5, not 3/5 (which would indicate pods are still starting). You can also use kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-web to see all 5 pods.

🔬 Practice Drill 4.1 — Wire It Together & Watch It Self-Heal

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Build a self-healing workload end to end — predict each result first:

  1. Create the easypj namespace + a Deployment (3 replicas).
  2. Expose it as a Service and confirm it has 3 endpoints.
  3. Delete one pod and watch the ReplicaSet replace it.
  4. Break the Service selector and watch endpoints go empty, then fix it.
Hint: A Service's endpoints are driven entirely by the selector↔label match — breaking the selector breaks routing even though the pods stay healthy.
View Solution
terminal
kubectl create namespace easypj
kubectl -n easypj create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3
kubectl -n easypj expose deployment easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000
kubectl -n easypj get endpoints easypj-web        # 3 pod IPs ✅

kubectl -n easypj delete pod -l app=easypj-web --field-selector status.phase=Running | head -1
kubectl -n easypj get pods -w                      # a new pod appears → back to 3/3

# break it: point the Service selector at a label no pod has
kubectl -n easypj patch svc easypj-web -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"nope"}}}'
kubectl -n easypj get endpoints easypj-web         # <none> — empty! 💀
kubectl -n easypj patch svc easypj-web -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"easypj-web"}}}'   # fixed ✅

Check yourself: the ReplicaSet self-heals to the desired count (owner links + reconcile loop), and a Service's endpoints are entirely driven by the selector↔label match — break that edge and traffic stops, even though the pods are perfectly healthy.

🔬 Practice Drill 4.2 — Roll Forward, Roll Back (Zero Downtime)

⏱️ Target Time: 7 minutes
Scenario

easypj-web runs 3 replicas of easypj:v1. Ship v2 with a rolling update, watch it complete, inspect the revision history — then discover v2 is buggy and roll back instantly. Finally, prove the old ReplicaSet machinery made the rollback cheap.

Hint: set image triggers the roll; rollout status/history/undo is the lifecycle trio. After the rollback, kubectl get rs shows the trick — the "old" ReplicaSet never died, it was just scaled to 0.
View Solution
roll → verify → undo → understand
# 0. Baseline (annotate the cause so history is readable)
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3

# 1. ROLL FORWARD to v2 — pods replaced in waves (maxSurge/maxUnavailable 25%)
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web easypj-web=easypj:v2
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web        # waits until the roll completes ✅

# 2. INSPECT the history
kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-web       # revision 1 (v1), revision 2 (v2)

# 3. v2 is bad → ROLL BACK instantly
kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-web          # or --to-revision=1
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web

# 4. THE TRICK — the old ReplicaSet was kept at 0 replicas the whole time
kubectl get rs -l app=easypj-web
#  easypj-web-6d8f9  3  3  3   ← v1, scaled back UP by the undo
#  easypj-web-7c4b2  0  0  0   ← v2, now parked at 0 for a future redo

Check yourself: a rollback isn't a rebuild — the Deployment just rebalances replicas between ReplicaSets it kept around (revisionHistoryLimit, default 10). That's why undo is instant and safe, and why the RS naming (-<pod-template-hash>) matters: one RS per template version. This exact sequence is a guaranteed exam task class.

🔬 Practice Drill 4.3 — "Running but No Traffic": the Readiness Cut-off

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Users say easypj is down, yet kubectl get pods shows all pods Running. Reproduce the classic cause: give a pod a readiness probe that fails, and watch Kubernetes silently pull it out of the Service — without restarting it. Then explain the liveness-vs-readiness distinction from what you observed.

Hint: Running is a phase; joining a Service requires the Ready condition. Watch kubectl get endpoints and the pod's READY 0/1 column — that's where the story is.
View Solution
break readiness → watch the endpoints drain
# 1. A deployment + service with a readiness probe that will FAIL
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=nginx --replicas=2 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > d.yaml
# edit d.yaml — add to the container:
#   readinessProbe:
#     httpGet: { path: /nope, port: 80 }   # 404 → probe fails
#     periodSeconds: 5
kubectl apply -f d.yaml
kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80

# 2. OBSERVE — Running, but 0/1 Ready, and the Service has NO backends
kubectl get pods                       # STATUS Running · READY 0/1  ← the tell
kubectl get endpoints easypj-web       # ENDPOINTS: <none>
kubectl describe pod -l app=easypj-web | grep -A3 "Readiness"
#   Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 404

# 3. FIX the probe path (path: /) and re-apply
sed -i 's|/nope|/|' d.yaml && kubectl apply -f d.yaml
kubectl get endpoints easypj-web       # pod IPs appear ✅ traffic flows
ProbeQuestion it asksOn failure
readiness"open for business?"remove from Service endpoints — no restart
liveness"alive at all?"restart the container
startup"still booting?"holds the other probes off until it passes

Check yourself: the pod never restarted (RESTARTS stayed 0) — readiness only gates traffic. The observable chain is: probe fails → Ready condition false → READY 0/1 → EndpointSlice drops the IP → users get nothing while the pod "looks" fine. That chain is the answer to one of the most common troubleshooting questions on the exam.

🔬 Practice Drill 4.4 — Namespaces: Isolation, Scope & Cross-NS DNS

⏱️ Target Time: 7 minutes
Scenario

Build the two-environment layout: namespaces easypj-dev and easypj-prod, one deployment in each. Then answer with commands, not opinions: (1) can two deployments share one name? (2) which resources ignore namespaces entirely? (3) how does a dev pod reach the prod Service by DNS?

Hint: Names must be unique per namespace, not per cluster. kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false lists the cluster-wide escapees. Cross-namespace DNS is the FQDN: svc.namespace.svc.cluster.local.
View Solution
two environments, one cluster
# 1. Two namespaces, same-named deployment in each — no conflict
kubectl create ns easypj-dev
kubectl create ns easypj-prod
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 -n easypj-dev
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v2 --replicas=3 -n easypj-prod
kubectl get deploy -A | grep easypj-web    # both exist — names are per-namespace ✅

# 2. What ignores namespaces? the cluster-scoped resources
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false | head
#   nodes · persistentvolumes · storageclasses · namespaces · clusterroles …

# 3. Cross-namespace DNS — short name inside, FQDN across
kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000 -n easypj-prod
kubectl run tmp -n easypj-dev --image=busybox:1.28 --rm -it --restart=Never -- \
  nslookup easypj-web.easypj-prod.svc.cluster.local   # resolves ✅
#   (plain "easypj-web" from easypj-dev would NOT resolve — wrong namespace)

# 4. Set your working namespace once instead of typing -n forever
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-prod

Check yourself: namespaces gave you name isolation, quota/RBAC boundaries, and DNS scoping — but not node, PV, or network isolation (nodes and PVs are cluster-scoped; traffic fencing needs NetworkPolicy, Ch 20). And deleting a namespace deletes everything namespaced inside it while cluster-scoped objects survive — the exact distinction api-resources --namespaced makes visible.

🔬 Practice Drill 4.5 — Label Surgery: Orphan a Pod, Watch the Controller React

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Labels aren't decoration — they're membership. Prove it: on a 3-replica easypj Deployment, change one pod's app label. Predict first, then observe: what does the ReplicaSet do? What happens to the relabeled pod? Then use the trick for what it's actually good for — quarantining a sick pod for debugging without losing it.

Hint: The ReplicaSet counts only pods matching its selector. Relabel one and the RS suddenly sees 2/3 — it creates a replacement. The relabeled pod keeps running, but now belongs to nobody (and left the Service too).
View Solution
membership is a label match
# 1. Baseline: 3 pods, all labeled app=easypj-web
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=nginx --replicas=3
kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-web            # 3 pods

# 2. SURGERY — relabel ONE pod out of the selector
POD=$(kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-web -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl label pod "$POD" app=quarantine --overwrite

# 3. OBSERVE — the RS instantly backfills; the orphan keeps running
kubectl get pods --show-labels
#   easypj-web-xxx-NEW    app=easypj-web   ← replacement (RS saw 2/3)
