#   easypj-web-xxx-OLD    app=quarantine   ← orphaned: still Running, out of the
#                                            Service, owned by nobody

# 4. WHY it's useful — debug the sick pod at leisure, no user impact
kubectl exec -it "$POD" -- sh                 # poke around the quarantined pod
kubectl delete pod "$POD"                     # clean up when done (nothing respawns it)

Check yourself: three deep facts surfaced at once — (1) a ReplicaSet's membership is the label match, nothing more; (2) the Service dropped the pod for the same reason (selectors again); (3) the orphan didn't respawn when deleted, because no controller claimed it anymore. The quarantine move — relabel to detach, debug, delete — is a genuinely useful production technique built entirely on Chapter 4's mental model.

📌 Chapter 4 Visual Summary — the objects, wired together
   🌍 Ingress/Gateway ─routes─▶ 🔌 Service ─selector(app=easypj)─▶ 📦 Pods
                                    ▲                                ▲ owned by
                               🚀 Deployment ─manages─▶ 🎛️ ReplicaSet ┘ creates (self-heal)
                                    │ pod template pulls in:
                                    ├─ ⚙️ ConfigMap / 🔒 Secret (envFrom)
                                    ├─ 💾 PVC ─▶ PV ─▶ 🧱 StorageClass
                                    └─ 🛡️ ServiceAccount ◀─ RBAC governs access
   🗂️ Namespace contains it all   ·   🧯 NetworkPolicy firewalls it   ·   🔖 LABELS are the glue
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   You create a Deployment → it owns a ReplicaSet → which owns Pods; a Service finds those Pods
   by LABEL and gives them a stable address. That sentence is 80% of every CKA workload task.

In words: The objects nest. You create a Deployment; it manages a ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet creates and self-heals the Pods. You never make the lower layers by hand — you describe the top one and ownership cascades down.

A pod's template pulls in everything it needs: ConfigMap/Secret for configuration (envFrom), a PVC → PV → StorageClass chain for storage, and a ServiceAccount (governed by RBAC) for API access. Out front, a Service uses a label selector (app=easypj) to find the ever-changing pods and give them one stable address; Ingress/Gateway routes external traffic to that Service. Around it all, a Namespace contains the objects and a NetworkPolicy firewalls them.

The takeaway: labels are the glue — nothing is wired by name, everything is matched by label. "Create a Deployment → it owns a ReplicaSet → which owns Pods → a Service selects them by label" is the single sentence behind roughly 80% of every CKA workload task.

🟢 Template Part 1 · Recap · Complete

Foundations — What You Now Know

You started unable to picture a cluster; now you can name every component, explain what breaks without each, trace a pod from kubectl apply to Running, and read any easypj manifest. That mental model is the platform the rest of the guide builds on.

🔑 Template Part 1 — Key Takeaways

  • Kubernetes automates deploy / scale / heal via desired-state reconciliation — you declare, control loops deliver (Ch 1).
  • Containers share the host kernel (namespaces + cgroups + union FS); K8s runs them via the CRI, not Docker (Ch 2).
  • Control plane = apiserver + etcd + scheduler + controller-manager; nodes = kubelet + kube-proxy + runtime. Only the apiserver talks to etcd (Ch 3).
  • Core objects: Pod < ReplicaSet < Deployment; Service for stable networking; Namespace for isolation; labels wire it all together (Ch 4).
  • 🎯 Exam: "which component?" thinking powers the whole 25% Architecture + 30% Troubleshooting domains.
  • 🔑 cluster-info · get nodes -o wide · api-resources · explain · crictl
📌 Template Part 1 Visual Summary — easypj source → image → desired state → running pods
   🐍 easypj source ─build─▶ 📀 easypj:v1 ─push─▶ 🏪 registry        (Ch 2: the unit)
                                                     │ pull
   📝 deploy.yaml ──kubectl apply──▶ 📡 apiserver ──▶ 🗄️ etcd          (Ch 1: declare desired)
   (replicas: 3)                       │ authN/Z/admit  (desired state)
                                       ├─ 🔄 controllers: Deployment→ReplicaSet→Pods
                                       └─ 📋 scheduler: bind each Pod → a node       (Ch 3: the brain)
                                              ▼
                            🤖 kubelet ─🐋 run─▶ 📦📦📦 easypj pods ─🌐 CNI gives IPs   (Ch 3: the muscle)
                                              ▼
                            🔌 Service (selector app=easypj) ─load-balances─▶ the pods   (Ch 4: stable net)
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   one app, described as desired state, that the cluster keeps alive — heal, scale, roll out, repeat. ☸️

In words: You build the easypj app into an image (easypj:v1) and push it to a registry — that image is the portable unit of deployment (Ch 2). You then declare what you want in deploy.yaml (e.g. 3 replicas) and run kubectl apply: the apiserver authenticates, authorizes, and admits the request, then writes that desired state into etcd — the single source of truth (Ch 1).

From there the cluster's brain takes over (Ch 3): controllers expand Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods, and the scheduler picks a node for each Pod. On that node the muscle acts — the kubelet tells the container runtime (via the CRI) to start the containers, and the CNI hands every Pod an IP. A Service with selector app=easypj then gives those churning Pods one stable address and load-balances across them (Ch 4).

The one idea to keep: nothing here is a one-off command — it's all desired state the cluster reconciles toward, continuously. That's why it can heal a dead pod, scale on demand, and roll out a new version on its own. Master this loop and the other 13 parts are just variations on it.

🟢 Part 1 · Foundation

Think Like GitOps

Chapters 1–3 · Beginner · "What is GitOps, and why does it matter?"

🟢 Beginner 📖 3 Chapters ⏱️ ~5 hours 🎯 Foundational — pre-GitOps concepts

Before you can operate GitOps tools you must be able to see the idea in your head. Part 1 builds that picture from nothing: what GitOps actually is, the Git mechanics every later chapter assumes, and the handful of Kubernetes objects you'll deploy every single chapter from here on. This is the foundation in the truest sense — everything in Parts 2 through 9 (ArgoCD, FluxCD, security, production patterns) assumes you already think in the vocabulary built here. Candidates who struggle with the CGOA exam are almost never beaten by an obscure feature; they're beaten because their mental model of push-vs-pull is fuzzy, so they waste time re-deriving it under a scenario question. Part 1 makes that model automatic.

🎯 What you'll be able to do by the end: say GitOps's one-sentence definition out loud, draw push-based CI/CD next to pull-based GitOps and explain the security difference, use the Git operations (commit, push, revert, branch) every later chapter assumes, and recognize the 5–6 Kubernetes objects (Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Namespace) you'll see in every YAML example from Part 2 onward. You won't have deployed anything yet — that's Part 2's job (Ch5.5 gives you a first, thin taste of it).
🧠 Analogy: A Thermostat, Not a Light Switch

A light switch is push-based: you flip it, something happens once, and nothing watches it afterward. A thermostat is pull-based and continuous: you set a target temperature (Git), and the thermostat constantly checks the room and corrects toward that target — forever, with no human re-flipping anything. GitOps agents are thermostats for your cluster.

🧭 Before You Start: WITHOUT GitOps vs WITH GitOps
❌ WITHOUT GitOps ✅ WITH GitOps
Deploy = SSH in, run a script, hope you remember every step. Deploy = git push; an agent inside the cluster does the rest, the same way every time.
Config drift is invisible until something breaks in production. Config drift is detected automatically and can self-heal (Ch4).
Rollback = hope you kept a copy of the old config somewhere. Rollback = git revert — a provable, auditable command.
"Who changed this and when?" = ask around, check Slack history. "Who changed this and when?" = git log, always.

Chapter 1 · What is GitOps? — The Big Picture

easypj runs fine on your laptop with python manage.py runserver. The moment you have to deploy it to production reliably — every time, the same way, without a human remembering every step — you need a system that continuously keeps the cluster matching what you declared in Git. That system is GitOps, and this chapter installs the mental model every other chapter in this guide assumes.

1.1 The Problem GitOps Solves

Before GitOps: manual kubectl, SSH scripts, "it worked on my machine." With 10 developers and 50 microservices, that manual process becomes chaos — nobody can say with confidence what's actually running.

❌ BEFORE GITOPS

👨‍💻 Dev: "I deployed v2." 👩‍💻 Ops: "But I see v1..." 😰 "Who ran kubectl?"

Manual process: SSH into server → kubectl apply -f → check if it worked → pray nothing breaks.

✅ WITH GITOPS

👨‍💻 Dev: git push. 🤖 ArgoCD auto-syncs. ✅ "Git says v2 = v2 runs."

Automated process: commit & push → ArgoCD detects change → syncs automatically → health check auto-runs.

The 2 AM Deployment — a real GitOps story
  🕑 2:00 AM — PRODUCTION INCIDENT

  WITHOUT GITOPS:                       WITH GITOPS:
  😰 Wake up, laptop, VPN, SSH...       😴 Sleep through it — agent
  ⏱️ 30 minutes to rollback                auto-rolls back
                                         ⏱️ 0 minutes (automatic)

  THE MORNING AFTER: check Git history — "Ah, v1.2.4 had a bug,
  auto-reverted to v1.2.3 at 2:01 AM." Full audit trail, no human
  intervention needed.

The manual deployment nightmare has five recurring pain points: human error (wrong namespace), no audit trail ("who changed replicas from 3 to 1?"), configuration drift (Git says one thing, the cluster says another), credential exposure (a hacked CI pipeline has cluster-admin access), and slow recovery (which YAML file was the previous version?).

1.2 GitOps Defined — The Simple Explanation

📖 Official Definition

GitOps is a set of practices for managing infrastructure and application configurations using Git as the single source of truth. In plain English: instead of telling Kubernetes what to do, you tell Git what you want. A robot (ArgoCD/FluxCD) makes it happen.

🧠 Analogy: The Thermostat

You set your thermostat to 72°F (declare in Git). The thermostat reads 72°F (the GitOps agent reads Git), compares it to the room (compares to the cluster), and if they don't match, it turns on the heat/AC (applies changes) — checking again every few minutes (the reconciliation loop). You never touch the heater directly; you only ever change the thermostat.

The GitOps elevator pitch
  📝 YOU DECLARE (in Git):          🤖 GITOPS ENSURES:
  # deployment.yaml                 ✅ 3 pods running
  replicas: 3                ──▶   ✅ All using v2 image
  image: easypj:v2                 ✅ Health check passing

  App crashes?      agent detects & restarts     🔄
  Someone changes?  GitOps reverts to match Git  ↩️
  New version?      update Git, GitOps rolls out 🚀
  Bad deploy?       git revert, auto-rolls back  ⏪

  💡 Git = Desired State. GitOps Agent = ensures Actual State = Desired State.
🚢 Analogy: The Shipping Manifest

A shipping port's manifest document says "Container A → Dock 3, Container B → Dock 7"; the harbor master reads it and directs the cranes so the actual dock layout matches. Kubernetes works the same way: a Git repository's manifest says "easypj → Node 3, postgres → Node 7"; the GitOps agent reads it and applies it so the actual cluster matches. The harbor master doesn't "push" containers — it reads the manifest and ensures the port matches. That's pull-based, just like GitOps.

📍 Everything above is taught here informally, through analogy — Chapter 31 revisits "Declarative Description," "Desired State," and the rest of the official CGOA vocabulary with exam-precise definitions once you have the intuition this chapter builds.

1.3 Why GitOps Matters — 8 Key Benefits

📝
Audit Trail

Every change in Git history — git log shows who, what, when, why.

🔄
Auto-Sync

No manual kubectl — the agent auto-applies changes.

🔒
Security

No cluster creds in CI — the agent runs inside the cluster.

⏪
Rollback

git revert = instant fix, full history of every deployment.

👥
Collaboration

PR review for infra changes — same flow as app code reviews.

🩺
Self-Heal

Drift detected and auto-fixed the moment someone changes a live pod.

📊
Visibility

See what's deployed now — the ArgoCD UI shows status of all apps.

🚀
Velocity

Deploy faster with safety — no manual approvals needed.

Example (self-healing): a teammate manually scales easypj from 3 pods to 1. Without GitOps, it stays at 1 until someone notices. With GitOps, the agent detects the drift and scales back to 3 automatically — healing time is roughly one sync interval (~3 minutes).

1.4 GitOps vs Traditional CI/CD — Detailed Comparison

AspectTraditional CI/CD (Push)GitOps (Pull)
Deployment MethodCI tool pushes to clusterGitOps agent pulls from Git
Credentials LocationStored in CI pipeline (risk!)Inside the cluster only (safe!)
Rollback ProcessRe-run old pipeline jobgit revert + auto-sync
Drift DetectionNone (manual check needed)Continuous, automatic
Audit TrailCI pipeline logs onlyFull Git commit history
Self-HealingNoneAuto-revert detected drift
Disaster RecoveryManual restore from backupPoint Git at a new cluster
Security PosturePipeline = attack vectorGit + agent = minimal attack surface
Who Deploys?CI bot (push credentials)Cluster agent (pull config)
Push vs Pull — visualized with easypj
  TRADITIONAL PUSH:                        GITOPS PULL:
  1. git push easypj app code               1. git push easypj app code
  2. CI builds Docker image                 2. CI builds Docker image
  3. CI runs: kubectl apply -f              3. CI updates image tag in
     ⚠️ CI HAS CLUSTER ADMIN CREDS!            config repo → git push
  4. CI polls rollout status                   ✅ CI only has Git access
                                             4. ArgoCD (in cluster) detects
                                                the config change
                                             5. ArgoCD syncs the change
                                                ✅ Agent in cluster, no
                                                   external credentials

1.5 The Pull-Based Model — Why It's Revolutionary

The security advantage is structural, not incidental: in the push model, credentials capable of changing the cluster must live somewhere outside the cluster (the CI pipeline). In the pull model, the agent that can change the cluster runs inside it, and initiates its own outbound connection to Git — nothing external ever holds cluster-admin credentials.

Push vs Pull — detailed architecture
  PUSH-BASED (CI/CD)                      PULL-BASED (GITOPS)
  GitHub Repo ─▶ CI/CD Pipeline           GitHub Repo ─▶ CI/CD Pipeline
                    │ kubectl apply                         │ git push YAML
                    ▼                                        ▼
               K8s Cluster                              Git Config Repo
                                                              │ Pull & Sync
  ⚠️ Cluster creds in pipeline!                              ▼
  ⚠️ No drift detection                                 ArgoCD / FluxCD
  ⚠️ Manual rollback                                          │ Apply
                                                              ▼
                                                         K8s Cluster

                                          ✅ No creds in pipeline!
                                          ✅ Continuous drift detection
                                          ✅ git revert = instant rollback

Real scenario: if the CI pipeline itself gets hacked, in the push model the attacker inherits cluster-admin access immediately. In the pull model, the attacker can at most alter Git — which is reviewed, versioned, and reversible, and still can't reach the cluster directly.

1.7 The GitOps Workflow — easypj End-to-End Example

Complete GitOps flow for easypj
  👨‍💻 Developer changes jobpost/views.py
        │ git push
        ▼
  GitHub (App Repo: easypj/easypj) ──▶ GitHub Actions CI
                                          1. Test (pytest)
                                          2. Build (docker)
                                          3. Push (registry)
                                              │
                                              ▼
                                  4. Update Config Repo
                                  (image: easypj:v1 → v2)
                                  git push to easypj-config
                                              │
                                              ▼
                          GitHub (Config Repo: easypj/easypj-config)
                                              │ Pull & Sync (every 3 min)
                                              ▼
                                     ArgoCD (GitOps Agent)
                                  Detect v2 → compare v1 → roll out v2
                                              │ Apply
                                              ▼
                                   Kubernetes Cluster
                              easypj v2 · easypj v2 · easypj v2

The last step before ArgoCD syncs the change is always the same: CI updates the Kubernetes YAML in the config repo. That one Git commit is the entire handoff from "code changed" to "GitOps takes over."

1.8 GitOps for easypj — Your Project Structure

easypj uses the two-repo pattern: application source code and Kubernetes manifests live in separate repositories, so each can have different access controls and review processes.

📦 REPO 1: easypj/easypj (App Repo)

easypj/ Django project (settings.py, urls.py, wsgi.py), jobpost/ Django app (models.py, views.py, urls.py), Dockerfile, requirements.txt, .github/workflows/ci.yaml.

⚙️ REPO 2: easypj/easypj-config (Config Repo)

base/ (deployment/service/configmap/secret/ingress + kustomization.yaml), overlays/ (dev, staging, production), argocd/ (Application CRDs).

The two-repo pattern separates application source code (developer-owned) from Kubernetes manifests (ops-owned) — enabling different access controls and review processes for each.

Under the Hood — What Actually Runs the Reconciliation Loop?

The thermostat and pull-model analogies simplify one detail: the reconciliation loop isn't magic, it's a controller — a long-running process built on the same controller-runtime pattern every native Kubernetes component uses (the same pattern a Deployment controller uses to keep replica count correct). ArgoCD's Application Controller and Flux's Kustomize Controller both run this exact watch-diff-act loop, just against Git instead of only against the K8s API. That's why GitOps tools feel like "native Kubernetes" instead of a bolted-on script — architecturally, they are.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Thinking GitOps means "just store YAML in Git." Storing YAML in Git without an agent pulling and reconciling it is only step 1 of the 4 principles — it's not GitOps yet, just version control.
  • Confusing GitOps with CI. GitOps is the CD half only. CI (build, test, push image) still happens in Jenkins/GitHub Actions/GitLab CI exactly as before — GitOps replaces the deployment step, not the whole pipeline.
  • Assuming the config repo and app repo must be the same repo. The two-repo pattern (1.8) is a recommendation, not a requirement — but mixing them blurs who can approve what.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • If a CGOA question describes credentials sitting in a CI/CD pipeline, the answer is almost always "push-based, not GitOps" — flag it instantly.
  • Memorize the 4 principles in this order: Declarative, Versioned, Pulled, Reconciled — D-V-P-R.
  • "Agent runs inside the cluster" is the single fact that answers most GitOps-vs-traditional-CI/CD security questions.

🏋️ Practice Drill — Diagnose a Broken Deployment Story

Scenario

A teammate says: "I fixed the easypj outage by SSH-ing into the node and running kubectl edit deployment easypj-web, bumping replicas back to 3. All good now!"

Task: In your own words, explain what will happen the next time the GitOps agent runs its reconciliation loop, and which of the 4 principles your teammate's fix violated.
View Solution

If Git still says a different value, the agent will overwrite the manual edit — Pulled Automatically and Continuously Reconciled were bypassed.

Q1
What were the 5 pain points of manual easypj deployment discussed in 1.1?
Show Answer

Q2
Give the one-sentence definition of GitOps from 1.2.
Show Answer

Q3
Name 3 of the 8 key GitOps benefits covered in 1.3.
Show Answer

Any 3 of: audit trail, auto-sync, security, rollback, collaboration (PR review), self-healing, visibility, velocity.

Q4
What's the single biggest architectural difference between traditional CI/CD and GitOps, per 1.4?
Show Answer

Traditional CI/CD pushes changes into the cluster from an external pipeline; GitOps has an agent pull changes from Git instead — the direction of the connection reverses.

Q5
Why is the pull-based model more secure than push, per 1.5?
Show Answer

Cluster credentials never leave the cluster — the GitOps agent runs inside it and initiates its own connection to Git, so a compromised external pipeline gains no cluster access.

Q6
Per 1.6, name the two main GitOps tools this guide covers, plus two alternatives it mentions.
Show Answer

ArgoCD and FluxCD are the two main tools; Jenkins X, Rancher Fleet, and Carvel kapp are named as alternatives (any two).

Q7
In the easypj end-to-end workflow (1.7), what is the LAST step before ArgoCD syncs the change?
Show Answer

CI updates the Kubernetes YAML in the config repo (a Git commit changing the image tag) — that commit is the entire handoff to ArgoCD.

Q8
What does the two-repo pattern (1.8) separate, and why?
Show Answer

Application source code (app repo, developer-owned) from Kubernetes manifests (config repo, ops-owned) — enabling different access controls and review processes for each.

Q9
A teammate manually scales easypj-web via kubectl. If selfHeal is enabled, what happens at the next reconciliation cycle?
Show Answer

ArgoCD detects the drift between Git's declared replica count and the cluster's actual count, and reverts the manual change back to match Git.

Q10
Which official CGOA term (Chapter 31) names the abstract target "3 replicas of easypj-web" as opposed to the YAML file that expresses it?
Show Answer

Desired State — distinct from the Declarative Description, which is the written YAML artifact itself (Ch31.2).

2.1 Git Concepts You MUST Know

Repositories, branches, commits, merges, pull requests — plus one detail that matters more in GitOps than anywhere else: the commit SHA. Every sync, every audit-trail entry, every rollback is anchored to a specific SHA.

Git branching models compared — GitFlow vs Trunk-Based
  ❌ GITFLOW (NOT recommended for GitOps)
  main ──●────●────●────────────────────────●──
          \   /    /                          /
  develop──●──●───●───●──●──●──●──●──●──●───
            \     /    \     /
  feature/   ●───●      ●───●   (MANY long-lived branches)
  ⚠️ Problem: Too many branches, merge conflicts, drift

  ✅ TRUNK-BASED (Recommended for GitOps)
  main ──●──●────●────●────●────●── (SHORT-lived branches)
         /  /    /    /    /    /
  feat/  ●─●     ●─●  ●─●  ●─●   (merged in days, not weeks)
  ✅ Benefits: Always deployable main, less drift, faster
the GitOps Git toolkit
# Making changes
git add deployment.yaml           # Stage the change
git commit -m "Scale easypj to 5 replicas"
git push origin main

# Inspecting history
git log --oneline                 # See all commits
git log -p deployment.yaml        # See file history
git diff HEAD~1 deployment.yaml   # What changed last commit?
git show abc1234                  # See full commit details

# Rolling back
git revert abc1234                # UNDO a specific commit
git push origin main              # → GitOps agent rolls back!

# Tagging releases
git tag -a v1.2.3 -m "Release v1.2.3"
git push origin v1.2.3

2.2 Git Operations for GitOps

git commit, git push, git pull, git revert — plus git log as your audit trail, git diff for what changed between versions, and git tag for versioning releases (e.g. easypj-v1.0.0).

The daily GitOps flow
  MORNING: Check what's deployed
  $ git log --oneline -5
  abc1234 Scale easypj to 5 replicas (3 hours ago)
  def5678 Update image to v2.1.0 (yesterday)

  AFTERNOON: Make a change
  $ vim overlays/production/deployment.yaml   # replicas: 5 → 8
  $ git add . && git commit -m "Scale for holiday traffic"
  $ git push origin main
  → ArgoCD detects → syncs → 8 pods running ✅

  EMERGENCY: Rollback!
  $ git log --oneline   (find bad commit: abc1234)
  $ git revert abc1234  (creates UNDO commit)
  $ git push origin main
  → ArgoCD detects → syncs → back to 5 pods ✅
  ⏱️ Total time: 2 minutes (vs 30+ minutes manually)

2.3 The Config Repository Pattern

A "config repo" (e.g. easypj/easypj-config) holds Kubernetes manifests, separate from application source code. Structuring it well means a base/ directory plus per-environment overlays/.

📦 APP REPO (easypj/easypj)

Python source code, Django models, HTML templates, requirements.txt, Dockerfile. CI builds the image. 👨‍💻 Devs change this — 🔓 less sensitive.

⚙️ CONFIG REPO (easypj-cfg)

K8s YAML manifests: Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Ingress, Kustomize overlays, environment configs. GitOps deploys the app. 👨‍💻 Ops/SRE own this — 🔒 RBAC restricted.

💡 Key insight: code changes frequently; config changes less often but is more sensitive. Separate repos means different access controls and different review processes.

2.4 Git Hooks and Automation

Pre-commit hooks (YAML linting, schema validation) and pre-receive hooks (enforcing policies before merge) integrate directly with the GitOps pipeline.

.pre-commit-config.yaml in easypj-config
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/adrienverge/yamllint
    rev: v1.35.1
    hooks:
      - id: yamllint
        args: ['-d', 'relaxed']
  - repo: https://github.com/yannh/kubeconform
    rev: v0.6.4
    hooks:
      - id: kubeconform
        args: ['-strict', '-summary']
$ pre-commit install   # one-time, wires this into git commit
$ git commit -m 'Bump easypj-web replicas'
# EXPECTED OUTPUT:
yamllint.............................................Passed
kubeconform...........................................Passed
[main a1b2c3d] Bump easypj-web replicas

Invalid YAML or a manifest that doesn't match the K8s schema is rejected before it can even become a commit — catching mistakes locally, before a PR reviewer ever sees them.

2.5 Pull Requests in GitOps

PR review applies to infrastructure changes too — with a different checklist than a normal code review.

📋 easypj-config Pull Request Checklist
  • Does kubectl kustomize overlays/<env> render without errors?
  • Does argocd app diff show only the intended change?
  • Are resource requests/limits set on every container?
  • Are secrets referenced (not hardcoded) — Sealed Secret/ESO?
  • Does this change need a Sync Wave (Ch12) for ordering?
  • Is the image tag a specific digest/SHA, never :latest?
  • Has this been tested in dev/staging before targeting prod?
  • Is the commit signed? (required by branch protection, Ch6.3)

💡 This checklist becomes a real GitHub PR template by saving it as .github/pull_request_template.md in easypj-config — it then pre-populates every new PR's description automatically.

2.6 GitOps and easypj — Your First Config Repo

Hands-on: create the easypj-config repository on GitHub, add a first deployment.yaml, open a PR to change replicas from 2 → 3, and watch that change propagate via ArgoCD once merged.

Under the Hood — Why git revert Beats git reset for GitOps

git reset rewrites history — it needs a force-push, which is dangerous on a shared branch and usually blocked by branch protection. git revert instead creates a new commit that undoes the old one, so history stays linear and append-only — exactly what a GitOps agent watching a branch expects. That's also why branch-protection and signed-commit rules almost universally allow revert commits but block force-pushes: a revert is an addition, not a rewrite.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Editing a merged PR's YAML directly in GitHub's web UI instead of opening a new PR — bypasses required reviews and CODEOWNERS, defeating the audit-trail benefit from Chapter 1.
  • Putting the environment name in the branch name (env/prod) instead of a directory (overlays/production) — creates the environment-branches anti-pattern covered in 6.2, causing drift between branches.
  • Force-pushing to main to "clean up" commit history — rewrites the exact audit trail GitOps depends on; most config repos should block force-push entirely.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • If a question asks how to undo a bad production change, and the options include both a kubectl rollback and git revert, the GitOps answer is always git revert — it's the only one that keeps Git and cluster in sync.
  • Trunk-Based Development does not mean "no branches" — it means SHORT-lived branches merged within days, not committing straight to main.
  • A commit SHA is the ultimate audit key — git show <sha> answers "who changed this and why" faster than any UI.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 2)

the GitOps-native rollback
git revert <sha>
    # Creates a new commit undoing <sha> — the GitOps-native rollback.

git log --oneline -- <file>
    # Audit trail for one file — who changed it, when.

git diff HEAD~1 <file>
    # See exactly what the last commit changed before it syncs.

🧪 Chapter 2 — Lab Q&A (10)

Q1
Which Git concepts from 2.1 does every later chapter assume you already know?
Show Answer

Commit, branch, merge, pull request, and revert — the basic Git vocabulary GitOps operations are built from.

Q2
What Git operation from 2.2 is the GitOps equivalent of a Kubernetes rollback?
Show Answer

git revert — it undoes a bad change via a new commit, preserving full history, rather than editing the cluster directly.

Q3
Per 2.3, what does the Config Repository Pattern separate, and why does it matter?
Show Answer

It keeps Kubernetes manifests in their own repo (or clearly separated directory), distinct from application source code, so review and access control can differ between the two.

Q4
What does a pre-commit hook from 2.4 typically check before a commit is even allowed?
Show Answer

YAML syntax validity and schema conformance (e.g. via yamllint/kubeconform) — catching mistakes locally before a reviewer ever sees them.

Q5
Per 2.5, what should a reviewer specifically check in a GitOps pull request that they wouldn't check in a normal code PR?
Show Answer

Whether kubectl kustomize/argocd app diff renders cleanly, whether resource limits are set, and whether the image tag is a specific digest — not just whether the code logic looks right.

Q6
What does easypj's first config repo (2.6) actually contain?
Show Answer

Kubernetes manifests (or Kustomize base/overlays) describing easypj's desired state — no application source code.

Q7
Why does this guide recommend Trunk-Based Development over GitFlow for a GitOps config repo?
Show Answer

Short-lived feature branches merged within days keep main always reflecting the deployable state, minimizing the drift risk long-lived GitFlow branches introduce.

Q8
What is the security reason signed commits matter specifically in GitOps, more than in a typical software repo?
Show Answer

Because Git IS the deployment trigger in GitOps — an unsigned or spoofed commit could trigger a real deployment, not just merge into source code.

Q9
If a config repo's pre-commit hook is skipped locally via --no-verify, what layer from Chapter 24 still catches an invalid manifest?
Show Answer

CI-level validation (a required status check) or, for secrets specifically, GitHub's native push protection — both operate independently of whether a developer's local hook ran.

Q10
What official CGOA term (Ch32.1) describes what this whole chapter is teaching — storing configuration as versioned text?
Show Answer

Configuration as Code (CaC) — GitOps is CaC plus automated pulling and continuous reconciliation on top.

3.1 K8s Concepts You Need for GitOps

You don't need the full breadth of Kubernetes for GitOps — you need a handful of objects GitOps YAML repeatedly declares: Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Ingress.

K8s ObjectFile in Git RepoWhat It Does
Deploymentdeployment.yaml"Run 3 easypj"
Serviceservice.yaml"Expose port 80"
ConfigMapconfigmap.yaml"Use these envs"
Secretsecret.yaml (sealed!)"DB password"
Ingressingress.yaml"Route traffic"
Namespacenamespace.yaml"Isolate envs"
PersistentVolumepvc.yaml"Store data"
HPAhpa.yaml"Auto-scale"
NetworkPolicynetpol.yaml"Restrict access"

3.2 Imperative vs Declarative — The GitOps Mindset

Imperative: "kubectl run nginx — create this now." Declarative: "I want 3 nginx pods" (written in YAML). GitOps requires declarative configuration — an imperative command Git doesn't know about gets silently overwritten on the next sync.

❌ IMPERATIVE (not GitOps-compatible)

$ kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5
⚠️ Git doesn't know about this change! Next sync → overwrites back to 3 (Git says 3).

✅ DECLARATIVE (the GitOps way)

Edit deployment.yaml: replicas: 3 → 5, then git commit && git push. Agent: "Git says 5 → cluster has 3 → fixing..." Git = Reality, always in sync.

💡 Rule: if it doesn't start with a Git commit, it's not GitOps.

The GitOps declarative stack
  Layer 1: Git Repository (Source of Truth)
    /easypj-config/
      base/deployment.yaml     ← "I want 3 easypj"
      base/service.yaml        ← "on port 8000"
      overlays/production/     ← "with these settings"
         │  GitOps Agent (ArgoCD/Flux) reads this
         ▼
  Layer 2: Kubernetes Cluster (Actual State)
    kubectl get all -n easypj-prod
    pod/easypj-abc123   1/1   Running   ← matches!
    pod/easypj-def456   1/1   Running   ← matches!
    pod/easypj-ghi789   1/1   Running   ← matches!

  💡 If Layer 1 ≠ Layer 2 → GitOps agent fixes it!

3.3 YAML Deep Dive for GitOps

YAML syntax essentials — indentation, lists, dictionaries — plus the pitfalls that bite in GitOps specifically, where a malformed manifest fails silently at sync time rather than immediately.

annotated deployment.yaml for easypj
# deployment.yaml — The heart of your GitOps config
apiVersion: apps/v1           # ← K8s API version
kind: Deployment              # ← Type of resource
metadata:
  name: easypj                # ← App name
  namespace: production       # ← Where it runs
  labels:
    app: easypj                # ← Labels for selection
    tier: backend
spec:
  replicas: 3                 # ← DESIRED STATE (Git says 3)
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj              # ← Which pods to manage
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: easypj
        image: registry/easypj:v2.1.0  # ← Version in Git!
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"

3.4 Kustomize — Config Without Templates

Kustomize is built directly into kubectl — no separate install. It layers per-environment patches on top of a shared base, using structural overlays instead of a templating language.

Kustomize overlay pattern — easypj environments
  easypj-config/
  ├── base/                     ← Common config for ALL envs
  │   ├── deployment.yaml
  │   ├── service.yaml
  │   └── kustomization.yaml    ← Lists resources
  ├── overlays/
  │   ├── dev/                  ← patches replicas: 1
  │   │   └── configmap.yaml    ← dev-specific settings
  │   ├── staging/               ← patches replicas: 2
  │   │   └── ingress.yaml      ← staging domain
  │   └── production/            ← patches replicas: 5
  │       ├── configmap.yaml    ← prod DB settings
  │       └── ingress.yaml      ← easypj.com domain

  HOW TO USE:
  $ kubectl apply -k overlays/dev         # Deploy to dev
  $ kubectl apply -k overlays/production  # Deploy to prod

  In GitOps: ArgoCD/Flux points to a specific overlay.

3.5 Helm — Package Manager for Kubernetes

Helm packages charts, values, templates, and releases — a versioned, distributable unit with a templating engine, closer to an installable package than a Kustomize patch.

FeatureKustomizeHelm
ApproachPatch-based (overlay)Template-based
Learning CurveEasy (just YAML)Moderate
Built into K8skubectl apply -kNeeds install
GitOps FriendlyExcellentGood
Best ForMulti-env, simple appsComplex apps, sharing configs
SharingCopy base directoryPublish chart repo
CommunityCNCF projects default1000s of charts

💡 Recommendation for easypj: use Kustomize for the easypj app itself (simple overlays); use Helm for PostgreSQL/Redis (community charts already exist). ArgoCD supports both natively.

3.6 Namespaces and Multi-Tenancy

Namespaces separate environments on one cluster: easypj-dev, easypj-staging, easypj-prod. ArgoCD manages all of them from a single Application Controller.

easypj namespace layout
  argocd namespace — ArgoCD Server manages ALL below

  easypj-dev            easypj-staging
  easypj: 1 replica      easypj: 2 replicas
  postgres: 1 replica    postgres: 1 replica
  🟢 Dev only            🟡 Pre-prod testing

  easypj-production
  easypj: 5 replicas (HA) · postgres: 3 replicas (StatefulSet)
  redis: 2 replicas · ingress: easypj.com
  🔴 LIVE TRAFFIC — restricted access
Under the Hood — Why kubectl apply -k Is Just Kustomize + kubectl apply

Kustomize isn't a separate program bolted onto Kubernetes — since kubectl 1.14 it's compiled directly into the kubectl binary. Running kubectl apply -k overlays/production does exactly two things: (1) kustomize build overlays/production renders the final YAML by merging base + patches in memory, then (2) a normal kubectl apply -f - runs against the result. ArgoCD's Repo Server does the identical two-step internally before ever touching the cluster — which is why anything you can kubectl apply -k locally, ArgoCD can sync, with zero surprises.

⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • Assuming Kustomize overlays "inherit and modify" YAML like a class hierarchy — they don't merge intelligently by default; a patch that targets the wrong resource name silently does nothing instead of erroring.
  • Storing a Secret's real value in Git "because it's just for dev" — Chapter 13 covers why even dev secrets need Sealed Secrets/SOPS; habits formed now carry into production.
  • Confusing a Namespace boundary with a security boundary — namespaces organize resources, they don't isolate network traffic without a NetworkPolicy layered on top.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • "Declarative = WHAT, Imperative = HOW" — if a CGOA question's kubectl command changes cluster state without a matching Git commit, it's imperative and it's wrong for GitOps.
  • Kustomize needs zero extra tooling (built into kubectl); Helm needs the helm CLI installed separately — a fast way to eliminate wrong answers on "which requires no additional install" questions.
  • Namespace-per-environment (easypj-dev / easypj-staging / easypj-production) is the pattern CGOA expects by default unless the question says otherwise.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 3)

Kustomize & Helm essentials
kubectl apply -k overlays/production
    # Render + apply a Kustomize overlay in one step.

kubectl get all -n easypj-prod
    # See every resource GitOps has deployed to prod.

helm install easypj ./easypj-chart
    # Install a Helm-packaged dependency (e.g. PostgreSQL).

🧪 Chapter 3 — Lab Q&A (10)

Q1
Which K8s objects does 3.1 say you actually need for GitOps, versus the full breadth of Kubernetes?
Show Answer

Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Ingress, Namespace — the handful GitOps YAML repeatedly declares, not deep cluster administration.

Q2
What is the core mindset shift in 3.2 from imperative to declarative?
Show Answer

Imperative says HOW to change something step by step (kubectl scale); declarative says WHAT the end state should be (replicas: 3 in YAML) and lets a controller figure out how to get there.

Q3
Why is kubectl apply considered idempotent, per 3.3?
Show Answer

Because it's declarative — re-applying identical YAML changes nothing, since actual state already matches desired state.

Q4
What problem does Kustomize solve without using a templating language, per 3.4?
Show Answer

It patches a shared base manifest per environment (dev/staging/prod) using structural overlays, avoiding the risk of templating text that isn't valid YAML yet.

Q5
What does a Helm chart package that a raw Kustomize overlay does not, per 3.5?
Show Answer

A versioned, distributable unit with parameterized values.yaml and a templating engine — closer to an installable package than a patch.

Q6
What does a Namespace provide for multi-tenancy, per 3.6?
Show Answer

A logical partition of one cluster — separate resource names, RBAC scope, and (with NetworkPolicy/ResourceQuota) separate resource and network boundaries per team or environment.

Q7
A manifest sets replicas: 3. Is this imperative or declarative, and why?
Show Answer

Declarative — it states the desired END STATE (3 replicas should exist) without specifying the steps to get there.

Q8
Why does this guide prefer Kustomize's overlay approach for easypj's dev/staging/prod split, per 3.4/3.6?
Show Answer

One base + three thin overlays avoids duplicating the full manifest three times, and keeps environment-specific values (replica count, image tag) isolated and easy to diff.

Q9
What's the risk of using Helm templating without understanding the rendered YAML underneath, connecting 3.3 and 3.5?
Show Answer

A templating error can produce syntactically invalid YAML that only surfaces at render/apply time — reading rendered output before committing avoids deploying broken manifests.

Q10
Which official CGOA term (Ch31.2) names the YAML file itself, as distinct from what it represents?
Show Answer

Declarative Description — the written artifact, as opposed to Desired State, the abstract target it expresses.

🟢 Part 1 · Recap · Complete

Foundation — What You Now Know

You started unable to explain GitOps in one sentence; now you can define it, diagram push vs pull, use the Git operations every later chapter assumes, and name the handful of Kubernetes objects every config repo declares. You haven't deployed anything yet — that's Part 2's job.

🔑 Part 1 — Must-Remember

  • GitOps means Git is the single source of truth, and an agent inside the cluster pulls from it — nothing pushes changes in from outside.
  • The 4 GitOps principles (Declarative, Versioned & Immutable, Pulled Automatically, Continuously Reconciled) are the exam's single highest-yield fact — memorize the order.
  • A Kubernetes Deployment doesn't run pods directly — it owns a ReplicaSet, which owns the Pods. You will see this ownership chain in every troubleshooting scenario later in the guide.
  • ⚠️ Gotcha: storing YAML in Git is step 1 of 4 — without automated pull and continuous reconciliation it's just version control. Git-layer commands (git revert) and Kubernetes-layer commands (kubectl rollout undo) operate on entirely different layers — Part 1 keeps these two toolchains straight before Part 3 combines them.
  • ⚡ Speed tip: credentials sitting in a CI/CD pipeline → "that's push-based, not GitOps" — answerable from Ch1 alone, no ArgoCD/FluxCD specifics required.
📌 Part 1 Visual Summary
▸ Push vs Pull
  The single most-tested distinction in the whole exam — an
  agent inside the cluster pulls, nothing pushes in.
▸ 4 Principles
  Declarative, Versioned & Immutable, Pulled Automatically,
  Continuously Reconciled — in that order.
▸ Git Mechanics
  Commit, push, branch, PR, revert — every later chapter
  assumes fluency here.
▸ K8s Toolkit
  Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Namespace — the
  objects every future YAML example uses.

In words: Part 1 built one mental model in three steps: why GitOps exists (an agent that pulls and reconciles, replacing manual push-based deploys), how it runs on Git (commit, push, revert, PR review, trunk-based branching), and where it lands (the handful of Kubernetes objects — Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Namespace — every config repo declares).

The one idea to keep: nothing in GitOps is a one-off command — it's all desired state in Git that a pull-based agent reconciles toward, continuously. Part 2 puts this model to work for the first time.
